quarrels.title: Aphrodite's birth

claims.claim: Aphrodite grew from the sea-foam that gathered around Uranus' severed genitals after Cronus castrated him, coming ashore at Cythera and Cyprus.
Aphrodite is the daughter of Zeus and the goddess Dione, into whose lap she falls for comfort after Diomedes wounds her at Troy.
Aphrodite is listed among Zeus's children, borne to him by Dione.

quarrels.significance: the goddess of love has two utterly incompatible origins — cosmic castration versus ordinary divine parentage — a clash so famous that later Greeks invented two separate Aphrodites (Ourania and Pandemos) to resolve it.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — all three positions exact against Perseus; Frazer's own footnote on Bibliotheca 1.3.1 flags the conflict with Hesiod.

quarrels.title: Hephaestus' conception

claims.claim: Hera bore Hephaestus entirely on her own, without union with any father, in angry rivalry with Zeus after he produced Athena from his head.
Hephaestus is the son of both Zeus and Hera, speaking of Zeus as his father and built the bedchamber Hera calls the work of "your own son."
Hera gave birth to Hephaestus without intercourse, though Apollodorus explicitly notes that Homer instead makes him a child of Zeus and Hera.

quarrels.significance: whether Hephaestus has a father at all changes the whole Olympian family drama — in Hesiod he is Hera's solo retaliation against Zeus, and Apollodorus himself flags the disagreement with Homer.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Apollodorus' wording confirmed nearly verbatim; minor nuance that Hesiod implies rather than states the Athena-birth motive (standard inference from the juxtaposition at Theogony 924–929).

quarrels.title: Ares' conception

claims.claim: Hera bore Ares to Zeus among the children of their lawful marriage — with Hebe and Eileithyia.
Ares is son of Zeus and Hera; Zeus reviles him as most hateful of the Olympians, with all his mother's unbearable spirit.
Juno conceived Mars with no father at all, touched by a magic flower from Flora's garden after Jupiter bore Minerva without her.

quarrels.significance: the Greek genealogical spine makes Ares an ordinary child of the royal marriage-bed, while Ovid's Roman calendar preserves a fatherless variant parallel to Juno's rivalry with Athena's head-birth — a secondary tradition, not Hesiod's or Homer's, but attested in our Ovid lens.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Hesiod and Iliad positions exact; Ovid Fasti passage confirms Flora's flower and fatherless Mars.

quarrels.title: Hephaestus' fall from Olympus

claims.claim: Zeus seized Hephaestus by the foot and hurled him from Olympus for taking Hera's side, and he fell all day before landing on Lemnos.
It was Hera who flung Hephaestus from heaven at birth, ashamed of his lameness, and Thetis and Eurynome rescued him in the sea.
Zeus cast Hephaestus out of heaven for coming to the rescue of Hera in her bonds, and the crash-landing on Lemnos is what lamed his legs.

quarrels.significance: Homer contradicts himself within the Iliad — two different throwers, two different landings — and the versions even disagree on whether the fall caused Hephaestus' lameness or his lameness caused the fall.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — both Iliad passages exact; caveat that "at birth" in the Iliad 18 version is standard scholarly inference (Homer says only that Hera wished to hide him for his lameness).

quarrels.title: Hephaestus' wife

claims.claim: Aphrodite is the wife of Hephaestus — caught in his net in the affair with Ares.
Hephaestus took as his wife Aglaea, youngest of the three Graces (Charites).

quarrels.significance: the smith-god is married to the goddess of love in Homer but to the youngest Grace in Hesiod — two different divine marriages that later authors never fully reconciled.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Odyssey 8 (the song of Demodocus) and Theogony 945 confirmed against the corpus.

quarrels.title: Eros: primordial force or Aphrodite's son?

claims.claim: Eros is one of the very first beings of the cosmos, arising alongside Chaos, Gaia, and Tartarus before any of the gods, "fairest among the deathless gods."
Eros is Aphrodite's unruly little boy, whom she bribes with a golden ball to shoot Medea with desire for Jason.
Cupid is Venus' winged son and the instrument of her power, shooting Apollo with the golden arrow and Dis at his mother's command.

quarrels.significance: Eros shrinks across the tradition from a cosmic generative force older than the Olympians into a mischievous child taking orders from his mother.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — quoted phrases match the Greek and Latin; the arrow strikes Medea slightly after the cited Argonautica range, but the claim only asserts the bribe, which is inside it.

quarrels.title: What came first

claims.claim: First of all Chaos came to be, with nothing before it, followed by broad-breasted Gaia, dim Tartarus, and Eros.
Chaos was not a being but a single shapeless disordered mass, which a god "and kinder nature" separated into sky, sea, and land.
Chaos itself has a parent: it was born from Caligo (Mist), and from Chaos and Caligo came Night, Day, Erebus, and Aether.

quarrels.significance: even the absolute starting point of the universe is disputed — Hesiod's unparented first entity becomes raw matter in Ovid and gets a mother in Hyginus.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Hyginus' "Ex Caligine Chaos" confirmed on ToposText; Ovid's "rudis indigestaque moles" and "deus et melior natura" confirmed in the Latin.

quarrels.title: Parents of the Fates (Moirai)

claims.claim: Nyx bore the Moirai — Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos — fatherless, among her dark brood of Doom, Death, and Nemesis.
The Moirai are daughters of Zeus and Themis, sisters of the Horae, "to whom wise Zeus gave the greatest honor."
By Themis, Zeus fathered the Fates: Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropus.
The Parcae — Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos — were born from Nox (Night) and Erebus.

quarrels.significance: Hesiod gives the Fates two different sets of parents within the same poem — a contradiction with stakes, since Night-born Fates stand outside Zeus's order while Zeus-fathered Fates are part of his regime.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — all four positions confirmed, including the "Atropus" spelling in Frazer; some editors suspect Theogony 217–222 of interpolation, a textual-criticism nuance that does not affect the claim.

quarrels.title: How the brothers divided the cosmos

claims.claim: The three sons of Cronus shook lots for the universe — Poseidon drew the grey sea, Hades the gloomy dark, Zeus the broad sky — with earth and Olympus held in common, so Poseidon insists he is Zeus's equal.
After the Titans' defeat the gods, at Gaia's prompting, urged Zeus to be their king, and he then distributed honors among the immortals himself.
After shutting the Titans in Tartarus, the brothers cast lots for the sovereignty, and Zeus was allotted the sky, Poseidon the sea, and Pluto the dominion in Hades.

quarrels.significance: random lottery versus elected supremacy is a real constitutional difference for Olympus — Homer's Poseidon can claim equality with Zeus, while Hesiod's Zeus rules by acclamation and hands out the portions himself.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — line-by-line check of the Greek of Iliad 15.187–193; Hesiod's acclamation-and-distribution wording exact at the cited lines.

quarrels.title: Who are the Cyclopes?

claims.claim: The Cyclopes are three sons of Uranus and Gaia — Brontes, Steropes, and Arges — divine craftsmen who forged Zeus's thunder and lightning in gratitude for their release.
The Cyclopes are a whole race of lawless, cave-dwelling shepherds without assemblies or ships, and their chief figure Polyphemus is a son of Poseidon.
Apollo slew the Cyclopes who fashioned Zeus's thunderbolt, in revenge for Zeus killing Asclepius.

quarrels.significance: Hesiod's three master-smiths and Homer's savage shepherd tribe cannot be the same beings — and Apollodorus has the smith-Cyclopes dead by Apollo's hand generations before Odysseus ever meets one.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified, citation corrected — the "no ships nor shipwrights" detail sits at Odyssey 9.125–129, just outside the originally cited range, so the Homer citation was extended.

quarrels.title: Atlas and the sky

claims.claim: Atlas, under hard constraint imposed by Zeus, stands at the western edge of the earth before the Hesperides, holding the broad sky on his head and tireless arms.
Atlas, the "baleful" father of Calypso who knows the depths of every sea, holds the tall pillars that keep earth and heaven apart.
Atlas was a giant king of the far west whom Perseus turned to stone with Medusa's head, his body becoming Mount Atlas on which the whole sky now rests.
Atlas is still alive and holding up the sky when Heracles — Perseus' great-grandson — comes seeking the apples of the Hesperides and briefly takes the burden onto his own shoulders.

quarrels.significance: beyond disagreeing on the mechanics (shoulders versus pillars versus mountain), Ovid's petrification by Perseus is chronologically impossible alongside the tradition that Perseus' descendant Heracles later bargained with a living Atlas.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — all four positions exact; the Heracles-as-Perseus'-great-grandson genealogy is confirmed by Apollodorus at Bibliotheca 2.4.

quarrels.title: Did Prometheus create mankind?

claims.claim: Prometheus is mankind's benefactor and Zeus's deceiver at the division at Mecone, but humans already exist and are never said to be his creation.
Prometheus moulded men out of water and earth, and also gave them fire hidden in a fennel stalk without Zeus's knowledge.
The son of Iapetus shaped man from new-made earth mixed with rainwater, moulding him in the likeness of the all-governing gods.
Prometheus, son of Iapetus, first fashioned men from clay ("Prometheus Iapeti filius primus homines ex luto finxit").

quarrels.significance: Prometheus-as-sculptor of humanity, now the standard image, is entirely absent from Hesiod, our earliest source — a striking case of a "core" myth that accreted centuries later.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Apollodorus and Hyginus confirmed verbatim; nuance that Ovid presents the Prometheus version as the second of two alternatives ("sive... sive..."), which does not affect the contradiction.

quarrels.title: Where did the human race come from?

claims.claim: The Bronze Race of men sprang from the ash trees — the Meliae, the ash-tree nymphs born of Uranus's blood.
Prometheus moulded men out of water and earth.
The son of Iapetus shaped man from new-made earth mixed with rainwater.
Prometheus, son of Iapetus, first fashioned men from clay.

quarrels.significance: Hesiod's anthropogony roots a race of men in the ash-tree nymphs, while the later mythographers credit Prometheus with moulding the first men from clay — two incompatible origins for mankind, with the Meliae appearing only in the Hesiodic version.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Hesiod Works and Days 143–147 (Bronze Race from the ash trees) and Theogony 187 (the Meliae born of Uranus's blood) confirmed in the local corpus; the Prometheus clay-moulding positions are exact per the entry above.

quarrels.title: Dionysus' first mother

claims.claim: Semele, daughter of Cadmus, bore Zeus a splendid son, Dionysus — a mortal mother bearing an immortal child.
Dionysus is the son of Zeus and Semele; when Semele was incinerated by Zeus's lightning through Hera's trick, Zeus sewed the six-month child into his thigh and bore him at term.

Liber was originally the son of Jove and Proserpina and was dismembered by the Titans; Jove gave his pounded heart to Semele in a drink, from which the god was conceived again — hence his epithet "the one with two mothers."

quarrels.significance: Hyginus preserves the Orphic "Zagreus" tradition in which Persephone, not Semele, is Dionysus' original mother — turning the familiar thigh-birth story into a rebirth.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Fabulae 167 matches every element including the two-mothers epithet; note that Hyginus places the thigh-sewing at Fabulae 179, not 167, but the position does not attribute that detail to him.

quarrels.title: Persephone's split year

claims.claim: Because Pluto gave her a pomegranate seed to eat, Persephone is compelled to remain a third of every year with him and the rest of the time with the gods.
Jupiter divides the revolving year into two equal parts (ex aequo), so Proserpina spends as many months with her mother as with her husband.
Ceres obtained from Jove that Proserpina spend half the year with her and half with Pluto.

quarrels.significance: the myth that supposedly explains the seasons cannot agree on its own arithmetic — a four-month winter in the Greek mythographic tradition versus the even six-month split of the Roman poets.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified, Ovid position tightened — claim re-worded to the Latin's "ex aequo... totidem menses" phrasing and the citation narrowed from 5.564–571 to 5.564–567, where the operative lines sit; Frazer's note on Apollodorus 1.5.3 flags this ancient disagreement.

quarrels.title: The parentage of Triptolemus

claims.claim: Triptolemus is the elder of Metaneira's children, to whom Demeter gave the winged dragon-chariot and wheat.
Triptolemus was a son of Eleusis, for Demeter came to him.
Triptolemus was a son of Ocean and Earth.

quarrels.significance: every author agrees on the mission — the boy who sowed Demeter's wheat over the world — but the genealogies split between an Eleusinian royal son, an eponymous Eleusis, and a primordial parentage through Ocean and Earth.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Apollodorus 1.5.2 records all three parentages in one passage; the dispute is attested only through his citation of Panyasis and Pherecydes.

quarrels.title: The mother of the Eleusinian Demophon

claims.claim: Demeter nursed the infant Demophon in the fire to make him immortal; when he grew marvelously by day, Praxithea watched, discovered him buried in the fire, and cried out — whereupon the babe was consumed and the goddess revealed herself.

The daughters of Celeus brought Demeter home from the Flowery Well, and Metaneira entrusted to her the rearing of her son — the queen whose cry broke the immortal rite in the fuller Eleusinian tradition beside Apollodorus.

quarrels.significance: the infant's name is stable in Apollodorus, but the queen who interrupted Demeter's fire-rite is Metaneira in the Eleusinian poets Pausanias follows and Praxithea in the Library's adjacent paragraph — a homonym hazard with the Athenian queen Praxithea wife of Erechtheus, whom the data keeps as a separate node.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 1.5.1 names Demophon and Praxithea in the fire ordeal; Paus. 1.39.1 assigns Metaneira the entrusted son without repeating the infant's name.

quarrels.title: The parentage of Adonis

claims.claim: Adonis was born when Lucina split the myrrh-tree into which transformed Myrrha had been changed after incest with her father Cinyras.
Cinyras in Cyprus married Metharme daughter of king Pygmalion and begot Oxyporus and Adonis among other children.
Adonis is listed among the youths whom Venus loved — in the Apollodoran royal genealogy, not the Ovidian tree-birth.

quarrels.significance: the same beloved hunter carries two incompatible origins — incestuous metamorphosis and myrrh-sap versus a lawful Cypriot royal marriage — and the atlas keeps both parent edges under the dispute topic rather than choosing one genealogy.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Met. 10.680–818 and Bibliotheca 3.14.3 confirmed against the pinned corpus; Hyginus Fab. 271 attests the love-story without resolving the birth.

quarrels.title: Pegasus in the Bellerophon myth

claims.claim: Bellerophon slew the Chimera on foot, trusting in the signs of the gods, with no mention of Pegasus.
Pegasus and noble Bellerophon together destroyed the Chimera.
Bellerophon mounted the winged steed, offspring of Medusa and Poseidon, and shot the monster down from on high.
At Corinth, Athena Chalinitis bridled Pegasus and delivered him into Bellerophon's hands for the kill.
He rode Pegasus to slay the Chimera and fell afterward in the Aleian plains, dislocating his hip.

quarrels.significance: the canonical image of the aerial Chimera-slaying depends on Pegasus, yet Homer's Iliadic genealogy knows only a foot-born hero trusting divine signs — the winged horse enters through Hesiod, Apollodorus, and local Corinthian cult.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Iliad 6.179–183 (no Pegasus); Theogony 325; Bibliotheca 2.3.2; Description of Greece 2.4.1; Fabulae 57.

quarrels.title: Where Persephone was taken and who told Demeter

claims.claim: Dis seized Proserpina as she gathered flowers by Lake Pergus near Henna in Sicily, and it was the nymph Arethusa who revealed to Ceres where her daughter had gone.
Pluto carried off Persephone secretly with Zeus's connivance, and Demeter learned the truth from the people of Hermione before quitting heaven in anger.

Greek localities anchored the myth to their own soil with competing descent-points rather than a Sicilian meadow: the Eleusinians showed Erineus beside their Cephisus as the spot where Pluto descended to the underworld after carrying off the Maid, while the Argives pointed to a circuit of stones by the river Cheimarrus near Lerna as the place of his descent with Kore.

quarrels.significance: cities across the Mediterranean competed to claim the abduction for their own soil, so the "same" story comes anchored to entirely different landscapes and informants.
quarrels.verification: corrected — the original draft misattributed an Attic seizure-site claim to Pausanias 1.38.5; that passage records only a descent-point at Erineus (and the Argive rival descent-point is at 2.36.7). Pausanias nowhere places the seizure itself in Attica. The Ovid and Apollodorus positions verified unchanged.

quarrels.title: Athena's parentage

claims.claim: Zeus swallowed his pregnant first wife Metis on the advice of Gaia and Ouranos (Earth and starry Heaven) and later himself gave birth to bright-eyed Athena (Tritogeneia) from his own head.
When the time of birth came, Prometheus — or, others say, Hephaestus — smote Zeus's head with an axe, and Athena sprang up fully armed from his crown.
The Libyans say Athena is the daughter of Poseidon and Lake Tritonis, which is why her eyes are sea-grey like Poseidon's.

quarrels.significance: Pausanias preserves a startling tradition making Athena the daughter of Poseidon — the very god she defeated in the contest for Athens — while the mainstream sources disagree about who wielded the axe at her head-birth.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified, Hesiod position refined — the original draft said "on Gaia's advice," but Hesiod attributes the advice to both Gaia AND Ouranos; the claim now names both advisers.

quarrels.title: Ariadne: slain by Artemis or wed to Dionysus?

claims.claim: Artemis killed Ariadne on the island of Dia, on the testimony of Dionysus, before Theseus could bring her to Athens.
Golden-haired Dionysus made Ariadne his wife, and Zeus made her immortal and unageing for his sake.
Bacchus rescued the abandoned Ariadne on Dia and set her crown among the stars as the Corona Borealis.
Theseus brought Ariadne to Naxos by night; there Dionysus fell in love with her and carried her off, and on Lemnos she bore him Thoas, Staphylus, Oenopion and Peparethus.
Theseus left Ariadne asleep on the island of Dia, and Liber, falling in love with her, took her from there as his wife.

quarrels.significance: Dionysus is the pivot of two opposite endings — in Homer his testimony gets Ariadne killed by Artemis, while in Hesiod and Ovid he makes her his immortal bride, and in Apollodorus and Hyginus he carries her off as his wife.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — the rare Homeric detail "Dionysou martyriesin" (by the witness of Dionysus) confirmed in the Greek; minor caveat that Ovid locates the crown between two constellations without naming "Corona Borealis," a standard identification. Epitome 1.9 (Naxos, carried off to Lemnos) and Fabulae 43 (left asleep on Dia, taken as Liber's wife) confirmed against the pinned corpus when the two entries for this topic were merged.

quarrels.title: Who turned Callisto into a bear?

claims.claim: Juno, enraged after the birth of Arcas, seized Callisto by the hair and turned her into a bear herself, and Jupiter later set mother and son among the stars.
Zeus himself turned Callisto into a bear to hide the affair from Hera, who then persuaded Artemis to shoot her as a wild beast — though others say Artemis shot her for failing to keep her maidenhood.
Juno in anger changed Callisto into a bear because she had lain with Jove, and Hyginus' star-myth handbook collects still more variants, including Diana killing the bear while hunting.

quarrels.significance: every retelling reshuffles the divine blame — Zeus, Hera, or Artemis as transformer or killer — making this a perfect case study in how the same constellation myth absorbed rival versions.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Astronomica 2.1 confirmed in the Latin to stack the additional variants (Diana as transformer per Hesiod's version; Juno transforming with Diana killing) exactly as claimed.

quarrels.title: Who fathered the children of Night?

claims.claim: Nyx bore Death, Sleep, Misery, Nemesis, Old Age and Strife without lying with any god.
Nox and Erebus together produced Death, Sleep, Wretchedness, Nemesis, Old Age and Discord.

quarrels.significance: Hesiod makes Night independently generative, while Hyginus turns the same powers into children of a paired male and female darkness.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified against the complete catalogues in Theogony 211–225 and the genealogical preface to Fabulae.

quarrels.title: Whose daughter is Ate (Ruin)?

claims.claim: Ate (Ruin) is one of the joyless brood that abhorred Strife (Eris) bore, alongside Toil, Forgetfulness, Famine and the rest.
Ate is the eldest daughter of Zeus, "she that blindeth all," whom he flung from Olympus by the hair after she deluded him at Heracles' birth.

quarrels.significance: Hesiod files Ruin among the abstract evils descended from Strife, while Homer makes her Zeus's own firstborn and tells the aetiology of her exile from Olympus to the heads of men.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified against Theogony 226–232 and Agamemnon's speech in Iliad 19.91–131.

quarrels.title: Is Oceanus a Titan child or the origin of the gods?

claims.claim: Oceanus and Tethys are children of Gaia and Uranus among the Titan generation.
Hera calls Oceanus the origin of the gods and Tethys their mother, placing the pair before the Olympian family order.
Oceanus and Tethys are Titans born from Earth and Sky.

quarrels.significance: the Homeric formula elevates the world-river and Tethys from members of one divine generation to the generative source of the gods.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified against the cited genealogical lists and both Homeric speeches of Hera.

quarrels.title: Who are the parents of Uranus?

claims.claim: Gaia bore starry Uranus by herself, equal to herself, to cover her on every side.
Caelus was born from Aether and Dies, alongside Terra and Mare.

quarrels.significance: Heaven changes from Earth's self-generated son and partner into a sibling of Earth produced by the bright upper air and Day.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified against Hesiod's opening cosmogony and Hyginus' genealogical preface.

quarrels.title: Who are the parents of Pontus?

claims.claim: Gaia bore the barren Sea (Pontus) by herself, without sweet union of love.
Pontus is reckoned a child of Gaia/Earth, who then with Pontus produces the sea-deities.
The Sea (Mare) was born from Aether and Dies, alongside Terra (Earth) and Caelum (Heaven).

quarrels.significance: the Sea mirrors the same cosmogonic split as Heaven — Earth's self-generated child in Hesiod, but a sibling of Earth produced by Aether and Day in Hyginus' Latin genealogy.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified against Hesiod's cosmogony and Hyginus' preface; the load-bearing Hyginus attestation is the "Earth, Heaven, Sea" triad of Aether and Dies (a separate doublet entry under Aether and Terra is the preface's known catalogue artifact).

quarrels.title: Who is the mother of the Iapetionids?

claims.claim: Iapetus took to wife the neat-ankled Oceanid Clymene, who bore him Atlas, Menoetius, Prometheus and Epimetheus.
Atlas, Epimetheus and Prometheus are children of Iapetus and Clymene — Menoetius is absent from the list.
To Iapetus and Asia were born Atlas, Prometheus, Epimetheus and Menoetius; his Oceanid catalogue opens with Asia and contains no Clymene.

quarrels.significance: the mother of Prometheus and Atlas is one Oceanid sister in Hesiod and another in Apollodorus — the disagreement is over which daughter of Oceanus and Tethys married into the house through which fire, the flood and the first woman reached mankind.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Theogony 507–514 and Bibliotheca 1.2.2–1.2.3 confirmed against Perseus, Hyginus' preface list ("From Iapetus and Clymene: Atlas, Epimetheus, Prometheus") against ToposText; the equation Clymene = Asia is a modern harmonization found in no ancient source.

quarrels.title: Where the thunderbolt sent Menoetius

claims.claim: Wide-seeing Zeus struck outrageous Menoetius with a lurid, smoking thunderbolt and sent him down to Erebus because of his mad presumption and exceeding pride — no battle is mentioned.
In the battle with the Titans Zeus smote Menoetius with a thunderbolt and hurled him down to Tartarus.

quarrels.significance: the two authors disagree both on where the blasted Titan fell (Erebus versus Tartarus) and on why — character in Hesiod (pure hubris), allegiance in Apollodorus (the Titanomachy).
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — both passages checked line by line; Hyginus' genealogical preface omits Menoetius from Iapetus' children altogether.

quarrels.title: Who was the first woman?

claims.claim: From the maiden moulded of earth — named Pandora in the Works and Days — is descended the race and tribe of women.
Pandora is "the first woman fashioned by the gods", mother of Pyrrha by Epimetheus.
On the pedestal of the Athena Parthenos is wrought the birth of Pandora, of whom Hesiod and others have sung that she was the first woman.
Pyrrha, daughter of Pandora and Epimetheus, "is said to be the first mortal created" (mortalis dicitur prima esse creata).

quarrels.significance: Hyginus shifts the primacy a generation down — as though the clay-born Pandora did not count as mortal, and humanity proper began with her daughter.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — the Latin of Fabulae 142 confirmed ("Inde nata est Pyrrha, quae mortalis dicitur prima esse creata"); Pandora is unnamed in the Theogony, named only in the Works and Days.

quarrels.title: Where the flood-craft landed

claims.claim: Deucalion drifts nine days and nights in a stocked chest, built on Prometheus' advice, and lands on Parnassus.
A little boat carries Deucalion and Pyrrha to the twin peaks of Parnassus, the only summit above the waves.
Deucalion and Pyrrha flee the cataclysm — no vessel at all — to Mount Etna, said to be the highest mountain in Sicily.
Parnassian local tradition agrees on the mountain: survivors of Deucalion's flood, led by wolf-howls, founded Lycoreia on its peak.

quarrels.significance: the Greek Ararat moves from Delphi's mountain to Sicily's volcano depending on the teller — and the means of survival changes with it (chest, boat, or bare flight).
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Fabulae 153's "in montem Aetnam, qui altissimus in Sicilia esse dicitur" confirmed against the Latin; Hyginus 152A ties the same flood to Phaethon's conflagration as Jove's pretext.

quarrels.title: One deluge or two? The Ogygian flood and Deucalion

claims.claim: In Boeotia the waters of lake Copais rose in the reign of Ogyges and inundated the whole valley; Attica too remembers an Ogygian flood after which the land was without kings until Cecrops.

The systematic flood narrative is Deucalion's alone: Zeus destroys the Bronze Age men, Prometheus' son rides out the waters in a chest, and mankind is refounded from stones — with no Ogygian deluge in the handbook.

quarrels.significance: local Greek memory preserved a primeval Ogygian catastrophe in Attica and Boeotia while the mythographer's spine runs straight to the Thessalian Deucalionid flood — so the atlas must show either one universal cataclysm or two stacked traditions, never silently merge them.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Pausanias 9.5.1 (Copais flood in Ogyges' reign) and 1.38.7 (Attic Ogygian flood) confirmed against Perseus; Apollodorus Bibliotheca 1.7.2 carries Deucalion only, with no Ogyges flood entry.

quarrels.title: Who ordered the stones thrown

claims.claim: The survivors consult the oracle of Themis by the Cephisus, and the goddess delivers the riddle of the great mother's bones.
Zeus sends Hermes to grant Deucalion whatever he chooses; he chooses people and throws the stones at the bidding of Zeus — whence laoi (people) from laas (stone).
The pair petition Jove directly to give them people or destroy them too, and Jove himself orders the stone-throwing.

quarrels.significance: the same act of stone-sowing is commanded by three different divine authorities — an oracle of the old order, a diplomatic Olympian messenger, or the direct voice of the sky god.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — all three repopulation mechanics confirmed against Perseus and ToposText, including Apollodorus' laoi/laas etymology.

quarrels.title: Were Deucalion and Pyrrha alone?

claims.claim: Sole survivors: "we two are the multitude; the sea holds all the rest" (nos duo turba sumus).
"The whole human race perished except Deucalion and Pyrrha" (omne genus humanum interiit praeter Deucalionem et Pyrrham).
All men were destroyed "except a few who fled to the high mountains in the neighborhood".
Local traditions name other survivors: Megarus swam to Gerania following crane-cries, and people woke to wolf-howls and escaped to the top of Parnassus, founding Lycoreia.

quarrels.significance: the poets need a world emptied down to one pious couple; the mythographer and the traveler keep the back doors open — every Greek town that claimed flood-surviving ancestors needed someone besides Deucalion to descend from.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — "nos duo turba sumus" confirmed at Metamorphoses 1.355; Apollodorus' "except a few" and both Pausanias local traditions checked against the primary texts.

quarrels.title: The father of Hellen

claims.claim: Hellen is the first child Deucalion had by Pyrrha — though "some say" his father was Zeus, a variant Apollodorus records in the same sentence.
Hellen stands in the catalogue of the sons of Jove: "Hellen by Pyrrha, daughter of Epimetheus"; the Astronomica likewise calls his son Aeolus a grandson of Jove.

quarrels.significance: whether the eponymous ancestor of all Hellenes is the son of a mortal flood-survivor or of Zeus himself decides whether the Greek peoples descend from human piety or divine blood.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — the children sentence sits at the end of Bibliotheca 1.7.2 (1.7.3 opens with Hellen's own sons), and Fabulae 155's Latin confirmed; Thucydides 1.3 and the Hesiodic Catalogue of Women, the other famous witnesses, are outside the seven-source set.

quarrels.title: Who gave fire to mankind?

claims.claim: Zeus hid fire, and Prometheus stole the far-seen gleam of unwearying fire in a hollow fennel stalk for mankind.
Prometheus gave men the fire he had hidden in a fennel stalk, without the knowledge of Zeus.
Prometheus brought fire down to men in a fennel stalk and showed them how to keep it banked in ash.

Beside the sanctuary of Apollo Lycius at Argos burns a perpetual fire called the fire of Phoroneus: the Argives do not admit that Prometheus gave fire to mankind, but assign its discovery to Phoroneus.

quarrels.significance: against the panhellenic fennel-stalk theft, Argos kept a rival civic claim — complete with an eternal flame as evidence — that the first fire was found, not stolen, and found by their own first man.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Pausanias 2.19.5 confirmed nearly verbatim ("they do not admit that fire was given to mankind by Prometheus, but insist in assigning the discovery of fire to Phoroneus").

quarrels.title: The mother of Phoroneus

claims.claim: Of Inachus and Melia, daughter of Ocean, were born sons, Phoroneus and Aegialeus.
Inachus, son of Oceanus, begat Phoroneus by his own sister Argia.
The Argive traditions he reports name no mother for Phoroneus at all.

quarrels.significance: the first man of Argos has an Oceanid mother named Melia in one handbook and Argia in the other — and Argia, like Melia, never appears outside her single genealogical sentence.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 2.1.1 and Fabulae 143 confirmed; Argia is listed among the Oceanids in Hyginus' preface, so both rival mothers are daughters of Oceanus.

quarrels.title: Whose daughter is Io?

claims.claim: Io is unambiguously the river Inachus' own daughter: he mourns her as lost, recognizes her as the heifer at his banks, and laments her fate.
Io's father was Iasus, son of Argus — though the annalist Castor and many of the tragedians make her a daughter of Inachus, and Hesiod (he reports) made her a daughter of Piren.
Io is born "from Inachus and Argia".
In the Argive king-list, Io who went to Egypt is the daughter of Iasus — yet before Deinomenes' statue on the Acropolis he writes "Io, the daughter of Inachus".

quarrels.significance: the most famous of Inachus' children may not be his at all — the paternity splits three ways across the sources, and Pausanias contradicts himself between books.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Apollodorus' triple report (Iasus / Inachus per the tragedians / Piren per Hesiod) confirmed at Bibliotheca 2.1.3; the "Hesiod says Piren" claim is Apollodorus' report of a lost work and must never be tagged to the hesiod lens directly.

quarrels.title: How did Danaus take Argos from Gelanor?

claims.claim: On arriving at Argos, the reigning king Gelanor surrendered the kingdom to Danaus.

Danaus claimed the kingdom against Gelanor son of Sthenelas; after both sides argued before the people, a wolf overcame a bull pasturing before the wall — and because Gelanor was like the bull and Danaus like the wolf, Danaus won and founded the sanctuary of Apollo Lycius.

quarrels.significance: Apollodorus treats the transfer as peaceful surrender; Pausanias preserves a contested trial decided by an omen — the same event, two very different tones for how the Danai dynasty began at Argos.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Apollodorus 2.1.4 and Pausanias 2.19.3–2.19.4 confirmed in corpus.

quarrels.title: Who recruited Myrtilus, and why did Pelops kill him?

claims.claim: Hippodamia, already in love with Pelops, persuaded Myrtilus to sabotage Oenomaus' wheels. Pelops later killed Myrtilus after the charioteer attempted to assault Hippodamia.
Pelops himself promised Myrtilus half the kingdom for sabotaging the chariot, then threw him into the sea because honoring the bargain would disgrace him.

quarrels.significance: the same treachery can make Hippodamia the architect and Pelops her avenger, or make Pelops both the corruptor and the faithless beneficiary. The curse of Myrtilus therefore begins from two different moral failures.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — both recruitment scenes, the omitted wheel pin, and the incompatible motives for Myrtilus' death were checked against Epitome 2.6–2.8 and Fabulae 84.

quarrels.title: How many Niobids were there?

claims.claim: Niobe had six sons and six daughters.
His own list has seven sons and seven daughters, but he also reports ten of each in Hesiod, two sons and three daughters in Herodorus, and six of each in Homer.
Niobe boasts of seven sons and seven daughters.
Amphion and Niobe had seven sons and seven daughters, followed by a named catalogue.

quarrels.significance: the scale and identities of the massacre change with the teller. A consensus sibling list would manufacture a family that exists in no ancient account.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Homer's total and Apollodorus' explicit source catalogue were checked against the primary texts; Ovid and Hyginus independently preserve the 7+7 version.

quarrels.title: Who survived the Niobid massacre?

claims.claim: His main account saves a son called Amphion and the daughter Chloris; the alternative attributed to Telesilla saves Amyclas and Meliboea.
All seven sons and all seven daughters die, followed by Amphion; Niobe is left childless.
Chloris is the only daughter to survive; Amphion later dies attacking Apollo's temple.

quarrels.significance: the massacre either annihilates the household or leaves descendants who connect Tantalus to Neleus and Nestor. The difference rewires an entire epic genealogy.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — the survivor names and Ovid's explicit childless ending were checked line by line. Chloris and Meliboea are not automatically merged because the source data does not yet support sourced aliases.

quarrels.title: Which sons did Atreus serve to Thyestes?

claims.claim: Atreus killed Aglaus, Callileon, and Orchomenus, sons of Thyestes by a Naiad, and served them to their father.
The victims were the infants Tantalus and Plisthenes; a later catalogue associates Thyestes' children with Aerope.

quarrels.significance: the catalogues disagree on the number, names, age, and maternal line of the murdered children. Combining them would turn two incompatible banquets into one oversized sibling set.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Apollodorus' three named sons and both Hyginus passages were checked against the primary texts; the contradictory mother in Hyginus remains prose-only until those children become entities.

quarrels.title: Who was the younger Tantalus' father?

claims.claim: The younger Tantalus, Clytemnestra's first husband, was a son of Thyestes.
He reports both Thyestes and Broteas as competing fathers.

quarrels.significance: the two placements attach Clytemnestra's first husband to different branches of the Pelopid house.

quarrels.title: What were Agamemnon's daughters called?

claims.claim: Agamemnon names Chrysothemis, Laodice and Iphianassa.
His catalogue names Chrysothemis, Electra and Iphigenia.

quarrels.significance: later tradition cannot safely turn Laodice into Electra or Iphianassa into Iphigenia without an explicitly sourced alias claim. Homer’s Laodice is entered as `laodice-atreid`, distinct from Laodice daughter of Priam.

quarrels.title: Who were Iphigenia's parents?

claims.claim: Iphigenia belongs to the household of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra.
She is Agamemnon's daughter and Orestes' sister.
He preserves the local claim that Helen bore Iphigenia to Theseus and entrusted her to Clytemnestra.

quarrels.significance: Pausanias' local tradition changes both Iphigenia's biological parentage and her place in the Atreid household.

quarrels.title: Who was Aegialia's father?

claims.claim: Aegialia is a daughter of Adrastus and Amphithea, listed beside Argia and Deipyle; Diomedes married her after taking Argos.
Diomedes' wife is Aegialeia, daughter of Adrastus.
Some say Diomedes married Aegialia daughter of Aegialeus, not of Adrastus directly.

quarrels.significance: the dispute shifts whether Diomedes' queen belongs to Adrastus' generation or to the fallen Epigon Aegialeus — and so whether the marriage secured the throne through the father-in-law or through the dead prince's line.

quarrels.title: Who was Cyanippus' father?

claims.claim: Cyanippus is a son of Adrastus and Amphithea, brother of Aegialeus.
The Biantid kings descended from Bias for four generations down to Cyanippus, son of Aegialeus.

quarrels.significance: Apollodorus makes Cyanippus Adrastus' son; Pausanias makes him Aegialeus' son and the last name in the Biantid succession — a one-generation gap that changes where the house of Bias ends.

quarrels.title: Who was Hippomedon's father?

claims.claim: Hippomedon is son of Aristomachus among the Seven against Thebes.
Some say Hippomedon was son of Talaus instead.

quarrels.significance: the variant collapses a generation and would make Hippomedon a brother's peer to Adrastus rather than a member of the next generation down through Aristomachus.

quarrels.title: Who was Amphilochus' father?

claims.claim: Amphilochus is son of Amphiaraus and Eriphyle, brother of Alcmaeon.
Amphilochus among the Epigoni is son of Amphiaraus.
An Amphilochus son of Alcmaeon came late to Troy.
Alcmaeon begot Amphilochus by Manto daughter of Tiresias.

quarrels.significance: the Epitome and Euripides variants collapse or restart the generation — making Amphilochus Alcmaeon's son rather than his brother — and so change whether he belongs to the Eriphyle matricide cycle or to Alcmaeon's later wanderings with Manto.

quarrels.title: Did Amphilochus share in the matricide?

claims.claim: Some say Amphilochus with his brother, others that Alcmaeon alone killed Eriphyle.

quarrels.significance: shared agency would bind both brothers to the Erinyes and to Pausanias' cult distinction at Oropos, where Alcmaeon is excluded from Amphiaraus' temple while Amphilochus retains his own altar-portion.

quarrels.title: Who killed Agamemnon?

claims.claim: Aegisthus is the principal killer, aided by Clytemnestra; Agamemnon also says Clytemnestra directly killed Cassandra.
Aegisthus and Clytemnestra jointly murder Agamemnon.
Clytemnestra and Aegisthus kill Agamemnon together.

quarrels.significance: the sources distribute agency differently, so a single unqualified killer edge would erase an important narrative distinction.

quarrels.title: Whom did Orestes marry?

claims.claim: He transmits alternatives in which Orestes fathers an heir by Hermione or by Erigone.
Orestes has Tisamenus by Hermione and Penthilus by Erigone.

quarrels.significance: Apollodorus frames rival successions while Pausanias incorporates both women into a divided line of descendants.

quarrels.title: Is Dione a Titaness or an Oceanid?

claims.claim: Dione is one of the Oceanid daughters born to Oceanus and Tethys.
Dione is one of the Titanides born directly from Earth and Sky.

quarrels.significance: Dione moves between two divine generations. The atlas keeps her visible as a Titan under the Apollodorus lens while rewiring her beneath Oceanus and Tethys under Hesiod.

quarrels.title: Who were Mnemosyne's parents?

claims.claim: Mnemosyne is a Titan daughter of Gaia and Uranus.
Mnemosyne is a Titanis born from Earth and Sky.
The transmitted genealogy makes Mnemosyne a daughter of Jove and Clymene.

quarrels.significance: Hyginus shifts Memory out of the first Titan generation and makes her a descendant of Zeus, an inversion that cannot be reconciled with the older genealogy.

quarrels.title: Who mothered the Sun, Moon and Dawn?

claims.claim: Theia bore Helios, Selene and Eos to Hyperion.
Thia and Hyperion are parents of Dawn, Sun and Moon.
Hyperion fathers Sol, Luna and Aurora by Aethra instead.

quarrels.significance: The same three celestial children receive a different mother in Hyginus. Aethra remains prose-only until her identity can be disambiguated and added in a later verified batch.

quarrels.title: Who is the mother of Oedipus' children?

claims.claim: Oedipus unwittingly married his mother Jocasta and begat Eteocles, Polynices, Ismene and Antigone.
Oedipus begat on Jocasta Eteocles, Polynices, Antigona, and Ismene.

Relying on Homer and the lost Oedipodia, Pausanias claims Euryganeia, daughter of Hyperphas, was the mother of the children, arguing the incest was discovered too quickly for four children to be born.

quarrels.significance: Whether the great Theban children—Eteocles, Polynices, and Antigone—are the products of incest or a later, legitimate marriage fundamentally changes their tragic taint.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Apollodorus' and Hyginus' lists confirmed; Pausanias' explicit rejection of Jocasta in favor of Euryganeia confirmed at 9.5.11.

quarrels.title: Where did Oedipus die and where was he buried?

claims.claim: After exile Oedipus came with Antigone to Colonus in Attica, sat as a suppliant in the precinct of the Eumenides, was kindly received by Theseus, and died there not long afterwards.

In the Nekuia Oedipus still bears the woes the Avengers of a mother bring to pass; in the Iliad Euryalus son of Mecisteus came to Thebes for the burial of Oedipus when he had fallen and there worsted all the sons of Cadmus in the funeral games.

Within the Colonus precinct is a monument to Oedipus, whose bones he found were brought from Thebes; he rejects the dramatic death-scene of later poets, citing Homer's funeral games at Thebes as evidence the old poet knew a different ending.

quarrels.significance: Whether the blind king's last hour belongs to Attica or Boeotia — and whether his tomb at Colonus held a translation of bones from Thebes — splits the Epic-Cycle tradition from Homer's funeral games and from the later Athenian cult topography Pausanias records.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Apollodorus' Colonus death confirmed; Homer's underworld woes and Iliadic funeral games confirmed; Pausanias' monument, bone-transfer report, and explicit rejection of the dramatic account confirmed.

quarrels.title: Who was the father of Antiope?

claims.claim: Antiope was the daughter of Nycteus and Polyxo.
Reports a tradition that her father was the river god Asopus, citing the poet Asius.
Antiope is the daughter of Asopus, who boasted of sleeping in the arms of Zeus.
On Jason's cloak she is Antiope daughter of Asopus, yet Arete later names Nycteus as the father who plotted against her.
Jupiter, in a satyr's shape, fills Nycteus' daughter with twins.
Antiope is the daughter of Nycteus.

quarrels.significance: Whether the mother of the great Theban twin-kings was a mortal princess or the daughter of a river god reflects the competing local traditions of Thebes and Sicyon.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Apollodorus' claim confirmed; Pausanias' citation of Asius and local report of Asopus as father confirmed; Odyssey 11.260–262 and Argonautica 1.735–736, 4.1089–1090 line-checked in the Greek and Metamorphoses 6.110–111 in the Latin; Fabulae 7–8 in the corpus English and the Latin (Lingua Latina Legenda).

quarrels.title: Who is the mother of Nicostratus?

claims.claim: Claims that "according to some," Helen gave birth to a son named Nicostratus by Menelaus, in addition to Hermione.
Rejects Helen as his mother, explicitly stating that both Nicostratus and Megapenthes were bastards born to slave women.

quarrels.significance: Whether Nicostratus was the legitimate heir of Helen or a bastard like his brother Megapenthes affected his claim to the throne of Sparta after Menelaus' death.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Apollodorus' note of the alternate tradition confirmed; Pausanias' explicit rejection confirmed.

quarrels.title: How did Haemon die?

claims.claim: Haemon was the last victim devoured by the Sphinx before Oedipus arrived.
Haemon survived to become betrothed to Antigone, but committed suicide over her dead body when Creon condemned her.

quarrels.significance: Did Creon's son die as an innocent victim of a monster sent by Hera, or did he die by his own hand because of his father's tyrannical decree? This contradiction fundamentally changes the moral weight of Creon's tragedy.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Apollodorus' claim confirmed; Hyginus' (and Sophocles') claim confirmed.

quarrels.title: Who seduced Danae?

claims.claim: Notes an alternative tradition that Danae was seduced by her own uncle, Proetus, sparking the war between the brothers.
Zeus visited Danae in the form of a golden shower that poured through the roof into her lap.

quarrels.significance: This contradiction strips away the divine glamour of the Perseus myth, reframing the origin of the hero as a sordid dynastic scandal and the true cause of the war between Acrisius and Proetus.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Apollodorus' note of Proetus' seduction confirmed.

quarrels.title: Proetus' wife: Anteia or Stheneboea?

claims.claim: Proetus' wife who lusted for Bellerophon and sent the lying letter is named Anteia (Antia).
The same queen is Stheneboea, daughter of Iobates of Lycia, whom Proetus married when driven to Lycia.
Stheneboea, daughter of Iobates, falsely accused Bellerophon and later killed herself when he married her sister Philonoe.

quarrels.significance: Homer and the mythographers name Proetus' queen differently — Anteia in the Iliad, Stheneboea in Apollodorus and Hyginus — yet both traditions make her Iobates' daughter and the author of the sealed death-token; she must never be merged with the Arcadian Stheneboea whom Apollodorus elsewhere makes a daughter of Apheidas.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Iliad 6.155–170 (Anteia); Bibliotheca 2.2.1, 2.3.1 (Stheneboea); Fabulae 57.

quarrels.title: How did Perseus die?

claims.claim: Perseus peacefully exchanged kingdoms with Megapenthes, taking Tiryns and founding Mycenae while giving Argos to Megapenthes.
Megapenthes eventually murdered Perseus to avenge the death of his father Proetus.

quarrels.significance: Did the great Gorgon-slayer rule out his days in peace, or did the cycle of fratricidal blood vengeance finally catch up to him?
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Apollodorus/Pausanias peaceful exchange confirmed; Hyginus' murder claim confirmed.

quarrels.title: Who is the father of Europa?

claims.claim: Europa is the daughter of King Agenor and Telephassa, making her the sister of Cadmus, Phoenix, and Cilix.
Europa is the daughter of Phoenix, making her the granddaughter of Agenor and niece of Cadmus.

quarrels.significance: This is a classic clash between the Homeric tradition and later mythographers. If Europa is Phoenix's daughter, the timeline of the Phoenician royal house shifts entirely.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Homer's 'daughter of far-famed Phoenix' claim confirmed.

claims.claim: At the sack of Troy, Menelaus slew Deiphobus — Helen's third husband — and led Helen away to the ships.
Helen herself is counted among the women who killed their husbands, with Deiphobus son of Priam as her victim.
When the spoil was divided after Troy, Odysseus received Hecuba as his special award.
Some say Helenus received Hecuba instead, crossed with her to the Chersonese, and that there she turned into a bitch with fiery eyes — the place called Cynosema, the Dog's Tomb.
Apollo promised to teach her prophecy if she would grant his favours; she learned the art and refused him, so he deprived her prophecies of the power to persuade.
She fell asleep in Apollo's temple; when the god tried to embrace her she refused, and he made her true prophecies unbelievable.

quarrels.title: Daphne's transformation

claims.claim: Daphne prayed to her father Peneus and Earth to destroy or change the beauty that harmed her; before the prayer ended her own body became bark, leaves, branches, and roots — the laurel tree — while Phoebus crowned himself with her foliage.
When Apollo pursued Daphne daughter of the river Peneus, she begged Earth for protection; Earth received her and changed her into a laurel tree, and Apollo broke a branch and placed it on his head.

quarrels.significance: the laurel is common to both tellings, but the agent of change differs — in Ovid the nymph's prayer transforms her own limbs, while Hyginus makes Earth the receiver and shaper of the tree.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Metamorphoses 1.688–748 and Hyginus Fabulae 203 confirmed against the pinned corpus (ToposText).

quarrels.title: Idmon's parentage

claims.claim: He was not in truth the son of Abas, but Leto's son Apollo begat him to be numbered among the illustrious Aeolids; Apollo himself taught him augury.
Idmon, son of Apollo and the nymph Cyrene; some say of Abas, an Argive.

quarrels.significance: the Argonaut seer's paternal line forks between a divine begetting by Apollo — with Cyrene as mother in Hyginus' fuller roll — and a wholly mortal Argive father in the variant Hyginus records but Apollonius rejects.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Argonautica 1.139 and Fabulae 14 confirmed against the pinned corpus.

quarrels.title: Sterope and Oenomaus — wife or mother?

claims.claim: Sterope, a Pleiad, was married to Oenomaus.
On the pediment at Olympia, Oenomaus stands with Sterope his wife, one of the daughters of Atlas.
Oenomaus was the son of Mars and Asterope, daughter of Atlas.

quarrels.significance: the same Pleiad name binds Oenomaus either as husband or as son — Asterope and Sterope are the same figure under variant spellings, so the chariot-king's tie to the Atlantid line forks between marriage and parentage.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 3.10.1, Description of Greece 6.21.7, and Fabulae 84 confirmed against the pinned corpus.

quarrels.title: Which Ilus begat Laomedon?

claims.claim: A barrow in the plain was reared for Ilus, son of Dardanus; in Aeneas' recitation Erichthonius begat Tros, and from Tros three sons were born — Ilus, Assaracus, and Ganymede — and Ilus again begat peerless Laomedon.
Dardanus' elder son Ilus died childless; Erichthonius succeeded and begat Tros, whose son Ilus founded Ilium and begat Laomedon — two different men named Ilus in one stemma.

quarrels.significance: Homer's plain keeps a tomb of Ilus son of Dardanus while the royal roll makes Laomedon the grandson of Tros through another Ilus; Apollodorus resolves the clash by making the Dardanid Ilus a childless elder brother and the founder of Ilium a younger namesake.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Iliad 11.371–372 (Ilus son of Dardanus) against Iliad 20.230–236 and Bibliotheca 3.12.2–3 (childless elder Ilus; founder Ilus son of Tros) confirmed against the pinned corpus.

claims.claim: Troilus the warrior charioteer stands among the sons Priam mourns having begotten.
Troilus closes the list of Hecuba's sons by Priam, yet "this last she is said to have had by Apollo" — the hedge preserved against his own catalogue.
Troilus appears without comment in the roll of Priam's children.

quarrels.title: Who gave Pandora life?

claims.claim: Zeus orders Hephaestus to mix earth with water and to put in the moulded maiden "the voice and strength of human kind"; Athena's part is only to gird, clothe and teach her.
Vulcan, at Jove's command, made the woman's form from clay, and it was Minerva who gave it a soul (cui Minerva animam dedit); the other gods added their gifts.

quarrels.significance: the animating power passes from the smith-god to the war-goddess — in Hesiod Hephaestus breathes voice and strength into the clay and Athena merely adorns it, while in Hyginus the body is Vulcan's and the soul is Minerva's.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Works and Days 60–64 and the "cui Minerva animam dedit" of Fabulae 142 confirmed against Perseus and ToposText; the land-and-sea-creatures detail on the diadem (Theogony 581–584) is not used as data pending verification.

quarrels.title: Why Phrixus fled — the stepmother's plot or the false accusation

claims.claim: Phrixus is the son of Athamas of Boeotia by Nephele; his stepmother Ino contrives a famine by parching the seed-corn and suborns the Delphic messengers so that the oracle demands Phrixus be sacrificed to Zeus, forcing him to the altar and then to flight.

The flight has no stepmother's grain-plot: Cretheus' wife Demodice (others name her Biadice) desired Phrixus, son of Athamas, and when refused accused him falsely of assault, so that Cretheus persuaded Athamas to put the youth to death.

quarrels.significance: the same flight is driven by two different households' malice — Apollodorus' jealous stepmother Ino faking an oracle against Nephele's children, versus Hyginus' spurned Demodice, wife of Cretheus, framing the boy in a Potiphar's-wife pattern. The atlas keeps a single Phrixus node with both motives tagged to this topic.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 1.9.1 and Astronomica 2.20.2 confirmed against the pinned corpus; Hyginus' Demodice/Biadice variant and its Cretheus framing are explicit in the Astronomica passage.

quarrels.title: Where did the golden ram come from?

claims.claim: The ram with the golden fleece was a marvel Nephele had received from Hermes.
Argus tells how Phrixus the Aeolid reached Aea bestriding a ram which Hermes had made all of gold.
The gilded ram was no god-wrought wonder but the offspring of Neptune and Theophane.

quarrels.significance: whether the ram is a divine artifact from Hermes (Apollodorus, Apollonius) or a living animal sired by Poseidon on the transformed Theophane (Hyginus) changes the fleece from a god's gift into a beast of Poseidon's stock.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 1.9.1, Argonautica 2.1140–1145 and Fabulae 3 confirmed against the pinned corpus.

quarrels.title: Is Aeolus the patriarch the same as the keeper of the winds?

claims.claim: Two distinct men share the name: the Aeolid patriarch stands at the head of the mortal house (Sisyphus and the rest his issue), while the keeper of the winds in his floating isle is Aeolus son of Hippotas — never merged.
Retelling the Odyssey, Hyginus makes the wind-keeper himself "Aeolus, son of Hellen, to whom control of the winds had been given by Jove," lending the Aeolid patronymic to the lord of the storms.
Ovid draws the warden of the winds into the founder's orbit in the wandering-hero narrative, so that mortal founder and wind-king slide together.

quarrels.significance: the trunk of the broadest mortal house in Greek myth is, by a later confusion, fused with a minor wind-god — exactly the kind of same-name collision the source lens exists to keep apart.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Odyssey 10.1–2 names the wind-keeper "son of Hippotas"; Fabulae 125's "Aeolus son of Hellen" conflation confirmed on ToposText. Ovid Met. 14.223 calls the wind-king "Hippotades," so his role here is association, not an explicit renaming — the prose attributes the explicit equation to Hyginus alone.

quarrels.title: Why does Sisyphus roll the stone?

claims.claim: Odysseus sees Sisyphus in violent torment, heaving the ever-rebounding stone — but no cause for the punishment is given.
Sisyphus is punished because he betrayed Zeus: when Zeus carried off Aegina, daughter of the river Asopus, Sisyphus told her searching father where she had gone.

quarrels.significance: the most famous punishment in Hades comes with no stated crime in our oldest source; the betrayal-of-Zeus motive (and the cheating-of-Death tale, which is in none of the seven) accretes later.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Odyssey 11.593–600 gives the torment without cause; Bibliotheca 1.9.3 supplies the Aegina/Asopus betrayal.

quarrels.title: The mother of Jason

claims.claim: Aeson, son of Cretheus, had a son Jason by Polymede, daughter of Autolycus.
Aeson had wedded Alcimede, daughter of Phylacus (herself born of Clymene daughter of Minyas); she is Jason's mother.
Jason is the son of Aeson and Alcimede, Clymene's daughter — agreeing with Apollonius against Apollodorus.

quarrels.significance: the leader of the Argonauts has two different mothers across the sources — a clean parentage fork that re-wires the maternal line of the saga's hero.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 1.9.16 (Polymede) and Argonautica 1.45–47 / Fabulae 14 (Alcimede) confirmed.

quarrels.title: The mother of Patroclus

claims.claim: Patroclus, son of Menoetius, by Sthenele daughter of Acastus.
The mother of Patroclus was Periopis, daughter of Pheres.
The mother of Patroclus was Polymele, daughter of Peleus.
Patroclus' ghost names only Menoetius as father and the exile from Opus; the mother's name is unstated.

quarrels.significance: Apollodorus records three rival mothers for Achilles' comrade in a single passage — Sthenele of the Iolcan royal house, Periopis of the Pheraean line, or Polymele of Peleus' house — while Homer leaves the maternal line open.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 3.13.8 (Sthenele / Periopis / Polymele) and Iliad 23.83–90 (father only) confirmed against Perseus.

quarrels.title: Who was Minyas of Orchomenus?

claims.claim: Chryses son of Poseidon succeeded Phlegyas and begot Minyas, who built the treasury and begot Orchomenus the eponym.
Minyas son of Aeolus built long ago the city of Orchomenus bordering on the Cadmeians; Jason's mother Alcimede was born of Clymene daughter of Minyas.
The Argonauts were called Minyae because Jason's mother was a daughter of Clymene, daughter of Minyas.

quarrels.significance: the name-giving king of the Minyae is either a Boeotian descendant of Phlegyas through Chryses or an Aeolid founder — two genealogies that cannot share one parent without merging incompatible royal lines.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Pausanias 9.36.4–9.36.6 (Chryses → Minyas) and Argonautica 3.1077 (Minyas son of Aeolus) confirmed against Perseus.

quarrels.title: Why is Athamas driven mad?

claims.claim: Athamas loses the children of Ino through the wrath of Hera — a wrath rooted, elsewhere in Apollodorus, in his and Ino's rearing of the infant Dionysus, the son of Zeus by Semele.
Juno, jealous of Ino's pride in her divine foster-child and her good fortune, descends to the underworld and sends the Fury Tisiphone to madden Athamas and Ino.

quarrels.significance: the madness that destroys Athamas' house is bare "wrath of Hera" in one account, divine jealousy over the nursing of Dionysus in another — the same catastrophe with different theological causes.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 1.9.2 (simple Hera-wrath) and 3.4.3 (Dionysus-nursing), Ovid Met. 4.416–542 (Juno and Tisiphone) confirmed.

quarrels.title: How did Melicertes die?

claims.claim: In one account Ino threw the boy Melicertes into a boiling cauldron, then leapt into the sea carrying the dead child.
The maddened Ino snatches the living Melicertes and leaps with him from a sea-cliff into the waves — no cauldron.
Ino flung herself with Melicertes from the Molurian Rock; a dolphin bore the boy ashore, and as Palaemon he received the Isthmian honours.

quarrels.significance: the child whose death founds the Isthmian games dies by boiling cauldron in one telling and is carried alive into the sea in others — the difference between a horror and a sea-change into the god Palaemon.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 3.4.3 (cauldron) against Ovid Met. 4.519–542 and Pausanias 1.44.7–8 (the leap and the dolphin).

quarrels.title: The father of Pelias

claims.claim: Tyro bore Pelias and Neleus to Poseidon, who had come to her in the likeness of the river Enipeus.
Pelias and Neleus are the twin sons of Poseidon by Tyro.
Pelias is the son of Cretheus and Tyro — a mortal father in place of the god.

quarrels.significance: the usurper of Iolcus who launches the Argonaut voyage is a son of Poseidon in the mainstream and a son of the mortal Cretheus in Hyginus — the divine paternity that dignifies the antagonist is not universal.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Odyssey 11.253–254 and Bibliotheca 1.9.8 (Poseidon) against Fabulae 12 (Cretheus).

quarrels.title: The father of Aethlius

claims.claim: Aethlius is the son of Zeus by Protogeneia, daughter of Deucalion.
Pausanias records both: that Aethlius was a son of Zeus and Protogeneia, but adds that "they say Aethlius too was a son of Aeolus."

quarrels.significance: the founder of the Elean line hangs off Zeus in the mainstream account but is folded back into the Aeolid stock by a local Elean tradition — which, since he married the Aeolid Calyce, would make his marriage one between siblings.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 1.7.2 (Zeus + Protogeneia) and Pausanias 5.8.2 ("Aethlius too was a son of Aeolus") confirmed.

quarrels.title: The descent of Endymion

claims.claim: Calyce and Aethlius had a son Endymion — "but some say that he was a son of Zeus."
Endymion is the son of Aethlius, who was himself a son of Zeus and Protogeneia.

quarrels.significance: the eternal sleeper loved by the Moon is an Aeolid great-grandson through Calyce and Aethlius in the systematic genealogy, yet Apollodorus himself preserves the rival claim that Zeus fathered him directly.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 1.7.5 ("but some say a son of Zeus") and Pausanias 5.1.3 confirmed.

quarrels.title: The origin of Cecrops I

claims.claim: Cecrops, a son of the soil with a body compounded of man and serpent, was the first king of Attica; the country formerly called Acte he named Cecropia after himself.
Cecrops was born from the earth, half man and half serpent, and was the first to establish laws and marriage rites.
Actaeus was the first king of what is now Attica; when he died, Cecrops, the son-in-law of Actaeus, received the kingdom.

quarrels.significance: the founder of Athens is either the land's first autochthonous king or the successor of an earlier ruler Actaeus — a whole reign appears or vanishes with the teller, and Cecrops' marriage to Agraulus daughter of Actaeus sits awkwardly beside the soil-born genealogy.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 3.14.1 (autochthon, Cecropia); Fabulae 48 (earth-born); Description of Greece 1.2.6 (Actaeus first, Cecrops son-in-law) confirmed against the pinned corpus.

quarrels.title: The parentage of Amphictyon

claims.claim: Amphictyon, third king of Attica, was a son of Deucalion (and Pyrrha) — the second child after Hellen.
"Some say that Amphictyon was a son of Deucalion, others that he was a son of the soil" — an autochthon like the kings he ruled among.

quarrels.significance: the king who received Attica after Cranaus is either the flood-survivor's son — knitting the Athenian throne into the Deucalionid stock — or one more earth-born Attic autochthon, owing nothing to the line of Hellen. Apollodorus preserves both within his own pages.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 1.7.2 (son of Deucalion) and 3.14.6 ("some say… a son of the soil") confirmed; Pausanias 1.2.6 names him king and Cranaus' son-in-law without pressing the descent.

quarrels.title: The father of Theseus

claims.claim: Theseus is simply "son of Aegeus, a man like the immortals" — purely mortal paternity.
Aegeus lay with Aethra, "but in the same night Poseidon also had connexion with her" — the paternity left open.
Poseidon, not Aegeus, lay with Aethra on the island Sphaeria after a dream from Athena — the divine father.
Neptune and Aegeus both lay with Aethra the same night, but "Neptune conceded the child to Aegeus."

quarrels.significance: the founder-hero of Athens is the son of a mortal king, of the sea-god, or of both at once — a paternity the city itself never settled, half-claiming Theseus for the Aegean.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Iliad 1.265 (son of Aegeus); Bibliotheca 3.15.7 and Hyginus 37 (the same-night reconciliation); Pausanias 2.33.1 (Poseidon at Sphaeria).

quarrels.title: The Amazon mother of Hippolytus

claims.claim: Theseus carried off an Amazon whom he names Antiope and by her begot Hippolytus.
In the war's aftermath, Theseus killed Hippolyte — the rival name for the same campaign.
The Amazon campaign is told with the rival names in the tradition of the Attic war.
The Amazon whom Theseus carried off is named differently in competing accounts; he records the Amazonium and Hippolyte's tomb at Megara.

quarrels.significance: the warrior bride who bore Hippolytus is Antiope in Apollodorus' list, Melanippe in others, and Hippolyte in Simonides — three names for one captive, and she must never be merged with Antiope the Theban mother of Amphion.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Epitome 1.16 (Antiope and Hippolyte in the same passage); Fabulae 250; Pausanias 1.2.1, 1.41.7.

quarrels.title: The father of Odysseus

claims.claim: Odysseus is the son of Laertes; in the underworld Anticleia names Laertes' kindness and her grief for her son.
Ulysses sailed to Troy as son of Laertes and Anticlia.
Sisyphus seduced Anticleia while she delayed at his court; some writers accordingly call Odysseus Sisyphean for his shrewdness.

quarrels.significance: the man of many devices is either the legitimate son of Laertes or the fruit of Sisyphus' cunning — a paternity dispute that explains the epithet some authors applied to his wit.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Odyssey 11.85–96 (Anticleia, daughter of Autolycus, wife of Laertes); Epitome 3.12 (Laertes and Anticlia); Fabulae 201 (Sisyphus and Anticleia).

quarrels.title: The mother of Philammon

claims.claim: Chione, daughter of Daedalion, lay with Apollo and Mercury on the same night; to Phoebus she bore Philammon, famous for song and lyre, twin to Autolycus.
Apollo and Mercury slept the same night with Chione (or Philonis), daughter of Daedalion; by Apollo she bore Philammon, by Mercury Autolycus.
Apollo begat Philammon on Leuconoe, daughter of Lucifer (Hesperos).

quarrels.significance: the singer who founded the Lernaean mysteries is either the son of Chione in the famous twin-birth tale that links him to Autolycus and Odysseus' line, or the child of a different woman in Lucifer's house.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Metamorphoses 11.301–317 (Chione and twins); Fabulae 200 (Chione/Philonis and twins); Fabulae 161 (Leuconoe daughter of Lucifer).

quarrels.title: Penelope and Antinous

claims.claim: Penelope keeps faith for twenty years, beguiling the suitors with her weaving until Odysseus returns; Agamemnon's shade praises her prudent heart.
Some say Penelope was seduced by Antinous and sent away by Odysseus to her father Icarius; in Mantinea she is said to have borne Pan to Hermes.
The Mantineans say Odysseus cast Penelope out for paramours; she went first to Lacedaemon, then to Mantinea, where she died.

quarrels.significance: the queen of Ithaca is either the unmatched type of marital fidelity in Greek epic or a figure later slandered with an affair that Homer's poem refuses to tell.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Odyssey 2.93–110, 11.444–446 (faithful Penelope); Epitome 7.38 (seduced by Antinous, sent to Icarius, Pan by Hermes at Mantinea); Description of Greece 8.12.6 (Mantinean exile tradition).

quarrels.title: Penelope and Amphinomus

claims.claim: Penelope keeps faith; Amphinomus alone among the suitors wins her favour with his good manners, and Odysseus slays him at the bow-feast — not his wife.
Others say Penelope was seduced by Amphinomus and met her end at Odysseus' own hands on that account.

quarrels.significance: the prudent Dulichian suitor whom Homer marks for death while Penelope survives becomes, in another ending, the alleged lover whose betrayal costs the queen her life at her husband's hand — a slander even harsher than the Antinous exile tradition.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Odyssey 16–18, 22–23 (faithful Penelope, Amphinomus slain) against Epitome 7.39 confirmed against the pinned corpus (Perseus).

quarrels.title: How did Odysseus die?

claims.claim: Odysseus is reunited with Penelope, reconciled with Laertes, and survives the feud of the suitors' kin when Athena stays the slaughter.
Telegonus, son of Odysseus and Circe, unknowingly kills his father with a sting-ray barb when he comes to Ithaca; Penelope is taken to Circe and married to Telegonus.

Some say the kinsfolk of the slain suitors accuse Odysseus; Neoptolemus, hoping to gain Cephallenia, condemns him to exile; Odysseus marries the daughter of Thoas in Aetolia, leaves Leontophonus, and dies in old age.

quarrels.significance: the man of many wiles either dies in his bed on Ithaca after Athena's peace, is killed by the son he begot on Circe, or ends his days as an exile in Aetolia — three incompatible closures to the same homecoming.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Odyssey 23–24 (survival); Epitome 7.36–7.37 (Telegonus); Epitome 7.40 (Neoptolemus' judgment and Aetolian death) confirmed against the pinned corpus (Perseus).

quarrels.title: Odysseus after Ithaca: Thesprotian kingship

claims.claim: After reunion with Penelope and Athena's peace with the suitors' kin, Odysseus remains on Ithaca; Telemachus is his only named son by Penelope.

After sacrificing to Hades, Persephone, and Tiresias, Odysseus journeys through Epirus, marries Callidice queen of the Thesprotians, reigns and begets Polypoetes; when Callidice dies he leaves the kingdom to their son and returns to Ithaca, where Penelope has borne Poliporthes in his absence.

quarrels.significance: Homer closes with the king at home beside one son; Apollodorus sends him abroad again as a Thesprotian ruler and adds a second son on Ithaca — a post-homecoming chapter Homer never tells.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Odyssey 23–24 against Epitome 7.34–7.35 confirmed against the pinned corpus (Perseus).

quarrels.title: Whom did Erechtheus slay at Eleusis?

claims.claim: Erechtheus slew Eumolpus himself, the Thracian son of Poseidon who led the Eleusinians.
The man Erechtheus killed was Immaradus, son of Eumolpus; Eumolpus himself remained at Eleusis.

quarrels.significance: whether the Athenian king cut down the invading priest-king or only his son decides whether the founder of the Eleusinian Mysteries died in the war that the Mysteries' truce later commemorated.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 3.15.4 (Eumolpus slain) against Description of Greece 1.27.4 (Immaradus the victim, Eumolpus surviving).

quarrels.title: How Erechtheus died

claims.claim: Poseidon, whose son Eumolpus Erechtheus had slain, destroyed Erechtheus and his whole house.
At Neptune's request, Erechtheus was smitten with a thunderbolt by Jove (Zeus).
Erechtheus was simply killed in the battle with the Eleusinians, alongside Immaradus — no divine smiting.

quarrels.significance: the victor's death is the god's revenge in one telling, the king of heaven's thunderbolt in another, and an ordinary battlefield fall in the third — the same war won and lost three ways.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 3.15.5 (Poseidon destroys him), Fabulae 46 (Zeus' thunderbolt at Poseidon's request), Description of Greece 1.38.3 (killed in battle).

quarrels.title: The father of Ion

claims.claim: Xuthus, son of Hellen, married Creusa daughter of Erechtheus and by her had Achaeus and Ion.

In the genealogy Ion is plainly the son of Xuthus — yet Pausanias also records the Acropolis-cave tradition that Apollo met Creusa there, the version Euripides dramatizes in which the god, not Xuthus, is Ion's true father.

quarrels.significance: the eponym of the Ionians is the lawful son of the Hellene Xuthus in the systematic genealogy, but an Attic cult-tradition makes him secretly Apollo's — turning Athens itself, not Thessaly, into the cradle of the Ionian race.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 1.7.3 (Xuthus the father) and Pausanias 1.28.4 (Apollo met Creusa in the cave below the Acropolis); the explicit Apollo-paternity is Euripides' Ion, out of the seven-source set, so it is carried only as the Pausanias-reported cult tradition.

quarrels.title: The eponym of the Achaeans

claims.claim: The genealogical roll at the close of the Theogony (Tier-B roster, Th. 1000) names Achaea among Zeus' offspring in the ethnic eponym series — a feminine figure paired with Hellen and Dorus at Th. 1002.
claims.citation: Theogony 1000 (roster line; English corpus ends at Medea/Medeus in Evelyn-White)

claims.claim: The Achaeans take their name from Achaeus, son of Xuthus and Creusa daughter of Erechtheus — not from a daughter of Zeus.
Gives Achaeus a historical career: return to Phthiotis, sons in Argos, and the naming of Peloponnesian peoples before the Dorian return.

quarrels.significance: the Hesiodic roll preserves a feminine ethnic eponym in Zeus' catalogue, while the genealogists who map the post-flood division of Hellas make the name flow through the male hero Achaeus and the Athenian marriage of Xuthus — two incompatible founders for the same ethnonym.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 1.7.3 and Pausanias 7.1.2–7.1.7 (Achaeus line); Theogony 1000 Achaea entry follows project roster indexing (Hesiodic ethnic roll); no Pleiad mother for Achaea is named in the seven-source set.

quarrels.title: How many generations from Lelex to the eponyms?

claims.claim: Eurotas is the son of Lelex directly, by the Naiad Cleocharia — Myles is omitted.
Lelex's son Myles reigned next (the mill-inventor), and only on his death did his son Eurotas succeed — making Eurotas the grandson.

quarrels.significance: a whole reign of the Laconian king-list appears or vanishes with the teller — the foundation of Sparta is one generation deeper in Pausanias than in Apollodorus.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 3.10.3 (Eurotas son of Lelex) against Description of Greece 3.1.1 (Myles between them).

quarrels.title: Whose son is Perieres?

claims.claim: Perieres is a son of Aeolus, listed among the Aeolids who married Gorgophone.
"Many say that Perieres was not the son of Aeolus but of Cynortas, son of Amyclas" — the Spartan stemma.

quarrels.significance: the seam where the Aeolid stemma meets the Laconian one — Perieres belongs to Thessaly's house of Aeolus or to the Spartan line of Amyclas, and the marriage to Gorgophone (a Perseid) sits on whichever side the teller chooses.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Apollodorus himself reports both at 1.9.5 and 3.10.3 ("many say… of Cynortas").

quarrels.title: Whose son is Tyndareus?

claims.claim: Perieres by Gorgophone begat Tyndareus, Icarius, Aphareus and Leucippus.
Cynortas' son was Oebalus, and it is Oebalus (by Gorgophone) who fathers Tyndareus — the Spartan kings descend through Oebalus.
"Tyndareus, son of Oebalus."

quarrels.significance: an entire generation (Oebalus) is inserted or skipped between Perieres/Cynortas and Tyndareus, depending on whether the Aeolid or the Spartan king-list is followed.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 3.10.3 (Perieres) against Description of Greece 3.1.4 and Fabulae 78 (Oebalus).

quarrels.title: Whose son is Hyacinthus?

claims.claim: Hyacinthus is a son of Amyclas (by Diomede), brother of Cynortas, who died before his father.
Hyacinthus is a son of the later king Oebalus.

quarrels.significance: the youth Apollo loved is set a generation apart depending on the source — son of the founder of Amyclae, or of the king who later fathered Tyndareus.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 3.10.3 (Amyclas) against Fabulae 271 (Oebalus); Ovid (Met. 10) leaves the father unstressed.

quarrels.title: Who was Helen's mother?

claims.claim: Leda, wife of Tyndareus, bore Helen to Zeus (who came as a swan).
Zeus pursued Nemesis, who laid an egg merely brought to Leda; Helen's true mother is Nemesis, Leda only her nurse.

quarrels.significance: the most beautiful woman in the world is the daughter of a Spartan queen or of the goddess of retribution herself — and at Rhamnous Nemesis was worshipped as Helen's mother.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 3.10.7 (Leda) and Apollodorus' own "some say Nemesis" against Description of Greece 1.33.7 and Astronomica 2.8 (the egg).

quarrels.title: Was the Helen of Troy real?

claims.claim: Helen sailed from Troy with Menelaus and received Telemachus with him in Sparta — the queen at the feast is the same woman whose abduction began the war.
