According to some, Menelaus had only a phantom of Helen made of clouds until he discovered the real queen at the court of Proteus in Egypt.

quarrels.significance: the Returns shelf must hold two incompatible Helens — the wife who feasts in Lacedaemon in Homer's Odyssey and the cloud likeness some mythographers place at Troy while the true queen waits in Egypt.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Odyssey 4.1–356 (Helen at the Spartan feast) against Epitome 6.29 ("phantom of her made of clouds" / "discovered Helen at the court of Proteus").

quarrels.title: Who was Mopsus of Colophon?

claims.claim: Mopsus who defeated Calchas at Colophon is a son of Apollo and Manto.
Manto crossed to Asia, married Rhacius the Cretan, and bore Mopsus, who drove the Carians from the land.

quarrels.significance: the seer who outprophesied Calchas has two parentages — divine paternity through Apollo in the Returns contest, or colonizer lineage through Rhacius and Manto in the foundation tale of the Ionian coast.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Epitome 6.3 (Apollo and Manto) against Description of Greece 7.3.12 (Rhacius and Manto).

quarrels.title: Are the Dioscuri mortal or divine?

claims.claim: Castor and Polydeuces are both sons of Tyndareus by Leda — yet the earth holds them living on alternate days, honoured like gods.
Leda bore the two at a single birth in the house of Tyndareus.
Zeus and Tyndareus lay with Leda the same night: she bore Polydeuces (and Helen) to Zeus, Castor (and Clytemnestra) to Tyndareus — so one twin is immortal, the other mortal.

quarrels.significance: whether the Dioscuri are wholly Tyndareus' mortal sons or a split mortal/immortal pair is the very point of their myth — for it is Polydeuces' divine half that he shares with dead Castor so the two alternate between Olympus and the grave.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Odyssey 11.298–304 (both Tyndareus', alternating life) and Argonautica 1.146–150 (one birth in Tyndareus' house) against Bibliotheca 3.10.7 and Fabulae 77 (the split paternity).

quarrels.title: Who killed Phocus?

claims.claim: Peleus and Telamon together plotted against their half-brother Phocus, and one of them — in the lot that fell, Telamon — struck him dead with the quoit at the games; for the murder both were banished by Aeacus.
The Aeginetan and Phocian traditions weigh the guilt differently — Telamon protested before Aeacus that he had no hand in it, and the blame is variously fixed; both brothers go into exile.

quarrels.significance: the founding crime of the Aeacid diaspora — which sent Telamon to Salamis and Peleus to Phthia, and so seeded the two greatest Greek houses of the Trojan War — cannot agree on which brother's hand threw the fatal discus.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 3.12.6 (Telamon by the cast of the quoit, both exiled) against Pausanias 2.29.9–10 (Telamon's plea of innocence and the divided Aeginetan tradition).

quarrels.title: Idas, Apollo and the choice of Marpessa

claims.claim: Idas, mightiest of men, took up his bow against Phoebus Apollo himself for the sake of fair-ankled Marpessa.
Idas carried Marpessa off; when Apollo would have taken her, Zeus parted the rivals and let Marpessa choose — and she chose the mortal Idas, fearing the god would desert her when she aged.
The chest of Cypselus showed "Idas bringing back Marpessa, not unwilling, from Apollo."

quarrels.significance: a mortal who out-faces a god with the bow, and a woman granted the rarest thing in myth — the choice of her own husband, made against immortality.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Iliad 9.557–564 (Idas vs Apollo) and Bibliotheca 1.7.8–9 (Marpessa's choice) confirmed; Pausanias 5.18.2 (the Cypselus chest) corroborates the willing return.

quarrels.title: Whose son is Idas?

claims.claim: Idas is a son of Aphareus and Arene, the brother of Lynceus.
"But according to many, Idas was begotten by Poseidon."

quarrels.significance: the strongest mortal of his age is, in the rival tradition, no mortal at all but a son of the sea-god — which alone could explain a man bold enough to draw his bow against Apollo.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 3.10.3 carries both the Aphareus parentage and the "many say Poseidon" variant; Apollonius 1.151 names him an Apharetid.

quarrels.title: Whose son is Meleager?

claims.claim: Meleager is the son of Oeneus, king of Calydon — "Meleager, son of Oeneus."
Lists Meleager among the children Althaea bore to Oeneus, but adds "they say that he was begotten by Ares."
Oeneus and Mars (Ares) lay with Althaea in one and the same night, and from them Meleager was born.
Names him "Mavortius" — the hero sprung of Mars (Ares).

quarrels.significance: the boar-slayer of Calydon is, in the older epic, simply the son of mortal Oeneus; the later mythographers slip the war-god into his begetting, so that the hero whose temper destroys his own house carries Ares' blood. Apollodorus preserves both readings side by side.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Iliad 9.543 (Οἰνῆος… Μελέαγρος) and Bibliotheca 1.8.2 ("they say… by Ares") confirmed against Perseus; Hyginus 171 and Ovid Met. 8.437 ("Mavortius") corroborate the divine paternity.

quarrels.title: Whose daughter is Deianira?

claims.claim: Counts Deianira among the children of Oeneus and Althaea, yet notes she "is said to have been begotten by Dionysus."
Liber (Dionysus), received as a guest, lay with Althaea and begot Deianira, giving Oeneus the vine in recompense.

quarrels.significance: Heracles' fatal wife is, in the household reckoning, a princess of Calydon — but the same sources whisper that the wine-god, not Oeneus, fathered her, the night Dionysus paid for his host's hospitality with the gift of the vine.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 1.8.1 carries both the Oeneus parentage and the "begotten by Dionysus" variant; Hyginus 129 (Oeneus) tells the guest-friendship and Liber's begetting of Deianira, confirmed against ToposText.

quarrels.title: Whose son is Thestius?

claims.claim: Thestius is born to Demonice by Ares — "Demonice had Evenus, Molus, Pylus, and Thestius by Ares."
Citing the early poet Asius, makes Thestius the son of Agenor son of Pleuron, so that his fatherhood of Leda descends from the Aetolian house, not the war-god.

quarrels.significance: the father of Leda and Althaea — the hinge that joins Calydon to Sparta — is in one line the son of Ares, in the other a purely human Aetolian; the choice decides whether the Tyndarids and the boar-hunters trace divine or mortal blood through Pleuron's house.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 1.7.7 (Thestius by Ares) and Pausanias 3.13.8 (Asius: Thestius son of Agenor son of Pleuron) confirmed against Perseus.

quarrels.title: Who was Tydeus' mother?

claims.claim: Oeneus, having married Periboea daughter of Hipponous after Althaea's death, begot Tydeus by her — the dominant account.
"But Peisander says that the mother of Tydeus was Gorge, for Oeneus by the will of Zeus lay with his own daughter."
Names Periboea as the mother of Tydeus.

quarrels.significance: whether the father of Diomedes — the second-greatest Greek at Troy — was born of Oeneus' second wife or, in the darker strand, of Oeneus' own daughter Gorge, hides an incest at the root of the Aetolian hero-line. Apollodorus alone preserves both, crediting the Gorge version to the epic poet Peisander.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 1.8.4–5 carries the Periboea parentage and the Peisander/Gorge variant in the same passage; Hyginus 69–70 corroborate Periboea.

quarrels.title: Was Amphidamas a son of Aleus or of Lycurgus?

claims.claim: Amphidamas is a son of Aleus, brother of Cepheus and Lycurgus — a generation above the boar-hunters.
The Argonaut catalogue brings "Amphidamas and Cepheus, who held Tegea and the allotment of Apheidas, two sons of Aleus."
Amphidamas is instead a son of Lycurgus (son of Aleus), brother of Ancaeus, Epochus, and Iasus — a generation below.

quarrels.significance: the slip of one generation tangles the Tegean Argonaut roster — whether Amphidamas sailed beside his brother Cepheus or beside his cousin Ancaeus — and it follows from the same uncertainty over whether Aleus' sons or Lycurgus' sons were the Tegean crew of the Argo.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Pausanias 8.4.8 and Apollonius 1.161–164 make Amphidamas a son of Aleus; Apollodorus 3.9.2 makes him a son of Lycurgus, confirmed against Perseus.

quarrels.title: Whose daughter is Atalanta?

claims.claim: Atalanta is the daughter of Iasus the Arcadian by Clymene daughter of Minyas — exposed at birth because her father wanted sons, and suckled by a she-bear.
Elsewhere the same author calls the boar-hunt Atalanta "daughter of Schoeneus," the Boeotian.
Gives both: "Atalanta, daughter of Iasus and Clymene" (Arcadian) against the Boeotian Atalanta "daughter of Schoeneus" of the foot-race.

quarrels.significance: the huntress comes in two homelands — the wild Arcadian exposed to the bear, and the Boeotian runner of the golden-apple race — and the ancient mythographers, Apollodorus among them, never settle which Atalanta is which, sometimes splitting her in two and sometimes merging her.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 3.9.2 (Iasus/Clymene) and 1.8.2 (Schoeneus) carry both filiations; Hyginus 70 and 185 confirm the Arcadian and Boeotian parentages respectively, checked against Perseus/ToposText.

quarrels.title: Who won the foot-race and married Atalanta?

claims.claim: Melanion, the persistent Arcadian suitor, dropped Aphrodite's golden apples in the course, won the race, and so married Atalanta.
Hippomenes, great-grandson of Poseidon, wins Atalanta with the three golden apples of Venus; the pair, lying together in Cybele's shrine, are turned into lions.
Names Hippomenes son of Megareus as the victor of the apple-race and Atalanta's husband.

quarrels.significance: the one race won by cunning rather than speed has two winners — the Arcadian Melanion of the local tradition and the Boeotian Hippomenes of Ovid — the same doubling that splits Atalanta's own parentage between Arcadia and Boeotia.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Apollodorus 3.9.2 (Melanion) and Ovid Met. 10.560–707 / Hyginus 185 (Hippomenes) confirmed against Perseus.

quarrels.title: Who fathered Parthenopaeus?

claims.claim: Parthenopaeus is the son of Atalanta by Melanion — or, the same author adds, by Ares.
In the muster of the Seven he is "Parthenopaeus, son of Melanion."
Makes him the son of Meleager by Atalanta — folding the boar-hunt lovers into his begetting.

quarrels.significance: the youngest and fairest of the Seven against Thebes hangs his paternity on Atalanta's tangled love-life — the husband Melanion, the war-god Ares, or her boar-hunt companion Meleager — so that the hero's blood is claimed at once for the mortal, the divine, and the Calydonian lines.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 3.9.2 (Melanion/Ares) and 3.6.3 (Melanion) and Hyginus 70/99/270 (Meleager) confirmed against Perseus/ToposText.

quarrels.title: Whose child is Echidna?

claims.claim: Echidna, the half-maiden half-serpent, is born in the sequence of Phorcys and Ceto's monstrous brood (commonly read as their daughter).
Echidna is the daughter of Tartarus and Gaia (Earth).

quarrels.significance: the "mother of monsters" is rooted either in the sea (Phorcys and Ceto) or in the very abyss (Tartarus and Earth) — a difference between a marine and a chthonic origin for the dam of Cerberus and the Hydra.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Theogony 295–305 places her among the Phorcyad brood; Apollodorus 2.1.2 names Tartarus and Gaia, confirmed against Perseus.

quarrels.title: Whose child is Ladon, the apple-dragon?

claims.claim: The serpent that guards the golden apples is the youngest child of Ceto and Phorcys.
The apple-guarding dragon is the offspring of Typhon and Echidna.

quarrels.significance: the dragon of the Hesperides is either a sea-born Phorcyad like the Gorgons, or one more beast of the Typhon–Echidna litter beside Cerberus and the Hydra.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Theogony 333–336 (Ceto and Phorcys) and Apollodorus 2.5.11 (Typhon and Echidna) confirmed against Perseus.

quarrels.title: Whose child is the Chimera?

claims.claim: The Chimera is the offspring of Typhon and Echidna.
In the Theogony the Chimera's mother is left ambiguous — the antecedent "she" may be Echidna or the Lernaean Hydra named just before.

quarrels.significance: the fire-breathing hybrid is either another child of Echidna or, in the strict reading of Hesiod's lines, born of her own monstrous sister the Hydra — a knot in the brood's own genealogy.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Apollodorus 2.3.1 (Typhon and Echidna); Theogony 319–325 carries the Echidna/Hydra ambiguity, confirmed against Perseus.

quarrels.title: Whose child is the Nemean Lion?

claims.claim: The Nemean Lion was borne by Echidna to her own son Orthrus, and reared by Hera in the hills of Nemea.
The lion is the offspring of Typhon — or, the same handbook adds, it fell from the moon.

quarrels.significance: the invulnerable lion of Heracles' first labour is either the incest-born whelp of Orthrus and Echidna, a son of Typhon, or a thing dropped from the Moon — three irreconcilable origins for one beast.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Theogony 326–331 (Orthrus and Echidna, reared by Hera) and Apollodorus 2.5.1 (Typhon / the lunar variant) confirmed against Perseus.

quarrels.title: Whose child is the Sphinx?

claims.claim: The Sphinx (Phix) was borne by Echidna to Orthrus, sister-beast of the Nemean Lion.
The Sphinx is the daughter of Echidna and Typhon.

quarrels.significance: the riddling terror of Thebes descends either from the hound Orthrus or straight from Typhon himself — the same fork that splits her litter-mate the Nemean Lion, now reaching the figure already standing in the Theban sky.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Theogony 326–327 (Orthrus and Echidna) and Apollodorus 3.5.8 (Typhon and Echidna) confirmed against Perseus.

quarrels.title: Whose child is Scylla, the sea-monster?

claims.claim: Scylla is the child of Crataeis, who "bore her for a bane to mortals" — no father named.
Scylla is the daughter of Crataeis and Trienus, or of Phorcus (Phorcys).
Lists Scylla among the monstrous offspring of Typhon and Echidna.

quarrels.significance: the cliff-monster of the strait is variously a daughter of the obscure Crataeis, of the old sea-god Phorcys (sister then to the Gorgons), or one more of Typhon's brood — and a separate strand (Ovid) makes her no monster by birth at all, but a nymph whom Circe poisoned into the thing that haunts the rock.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Homer Od. 12.124–125 (Crataeis) and Apollodorus Epit. 7.20 (Crataeis/Phorcus) confirmed against Perseus; Hyginus' preface places her in the Typhon–Echidna litter.

quarrels.title: Who was Amphitryon's mother?

claims.claim: Alcaeus had Amphitryon and Anaxo by Astydamia, daughter of Pelops — but some say by Laonome, daughter of Guneus, and others by Hipponome, daughter of Menoeceus.
Amphitryon is son of Alcaeus by Laonome of Pheneus, daughter of Guneus, and not by Lysidice, daughter of Pelops.

quarrels.significance: three rival mothers within and across sources for the Perseid prince who married Alcmena; `astydamia-pelops` carries Apollodorus' primary reading only. Not Astydamia wife of Acastus at Iolcus (`astydamia-acastus`).

quarrels.title: Whose son is Heracles?

claims.claim: Alcmene "was joined in love with Zeus who drives the clouds and bare Heracles" — the divine sire.
On one night Zeus came to Alcmene in the likeness of Amphitryon, and the next Amphitryon himself returned; she bore Heracles to Zeus and Iphicles to Amphitryon.
Hera's trick at the birth has Zeus boast that the child of his blood born that day would rule — so Heracles is Zeus' son, cheated of Mycenae by Eurystheus.

quarrels.significance: the archetypal double-fatherhood — the same night gives Alcmene a god's son and a man's, the divine Heracles and the mortal Iphicles — so the hero is at once a Perseid prince and the son of Zeus, the tension that drives Hera's hatred and the whole career of labours.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Hesiod Theog. 526–532 (Zeus the father), Apollodorus 2.4.8 (the two nights, the twin paternity), and Homer Il. 19.95–133 (Zeus' oath and Hera's trick) confirmed against Perseus.

quarrels.title: What became of Erginus after the Minyan war?

claims.claim: Heracles armed the Thebans, routed the Minyans at the Cephisus, and slew Erginus; then he marched on Orchomenus and ended the tribute.
Heracles conquered the Orchomenians and their king Erginus son of Clymenus; Erginus made peace, later took a young wife by oracle, and begot Trophonius and Agamedes.

quarrels.significance: the Minyan king whom Heracles overthrew either dies in the rout that wins Megara for the hero or survives to rebuild Orchomenus and father the builders of Delphi's treasury — the same war, two incompatible fates for the same king.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 2.4.11 (Erginus slain) and Pausanias 9.37.3–9.37.4 (peace, late marriage, Trophonius and Agamedes) confirmed against Perseus.

quarrels.title: Whose son is Augeas?

claims.claim: Augeas was a son of the Sun, Helios — or, some say, of Poseidon (others of Phorbas), king of Elis and rich in herds.
Augeas, king of Elis, was reputed a son of Helios; his father is also given as the mortal Eleius, the name shifted from Helios.

quarrels.significance: the owner of the inexhaustible herds whose stables Heracles must flush is fittingly made a son of the Sun — the divine cattle-lord — though a rival tradition grounds him in Poseidon or in a mortal king of Elis, the glory of the solar descent against a plainer pedigree.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Apollodorus 2.5.5 carries Helios with the Poseidon/Phorbas variants; Pausanias 5.1.9 reports the Helios paternity and the Eleius rationalisation, confirmed against Perseus.

quarrels.title: Who killed Eurystheus?

claims.claim: When Eurystheus pursued the Heraclids and was routed in Attica, Hyllus pursued him and cut off his head.
The aged Iolaus, restored to youth for a day, captured Eurystheus and slew him (or took him alive to Alcmene, who put him to death).

quarrels.significance: the persecutor of Heracles' line falls at last either to the hero's eldest son Hyllus or to his old companion Iolaus, the two who carried Heracles' cause into the next generation — and Alcmene's vengeance on the captive caps the feud that began before Heracles was born.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Apollodorus 2.8.1 (Hyllus beheads Eurystheus) and Pausanias 1.44.10 / 1.32.6 (the rejuvenated Iolaus takes him) confirmed against Perseus.

quarrels.title: Birth order of the Hundred-Handers

claims.claim: The Hundred-Handers Cottus, Briareos, and Gyes are named last among the children of Earth and Heaven, after the Titans and the Cyclopes.
Sky, having wedded Earth, "begat first the Hundred-handed, as they are named: Briareus, Gyes, Cottus" — the very first-born, before the Cyclopes and the Titans.

quarrels.significance: the same three monstrous brothers are placed at opposite ends of the first generation — Hesiod's afterthought to the Titans against Apollodorus' first issue of Sky and Earth — reshuffling the whole opening of the cosmos and which children Uranus first feared and bound.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Hesiod Theog. 139–153 (Hundred-Handers named after Titans and Cyclopes) and Apollodorus Bibliotheca 1.1.1 (the Hundred-handed begotten first) confirmed against the pinned corpus (Perseus).

quarrels.title: When and why were the Gigantes born?

claims.claim: The Giants spring from the bloody drops of the castrated Uranus that fell upon Gaia — in the same gush that bore the Erinyes and the Meliae, at the moment of Cronus' deed against his father.

Gaia conceived the Giants by Sky (Uranus) and brought them forth in her wrath over the fallen Titans — a second revolt bred to avenge the older defeated race, not born from the castration wound itself.

quarrels.significance: the earthborn army of the Gigantomachy is either coeval with the very first violence of the succession myth — sprung from Uranus' blood alongside the Furies — or a later brood raised specifically to punish Zeus for overthrowing Cronus, shifting the war's motive from primal cosmic crime to dynastic revenge.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Hesiod Theog. 183–186 (Giants from Uranus' blood on Earth) and Apollodorus Bibliotheca 1.6.1 (Giants born of Gaia's wrath over the Titans) confirmed against the pinned corpus (Perseus).

quarrels.title: Whose children are the Erinyes (Furies)?

claims.claim: Gaia (Earth) brought forth the strong Erinyes from the bloody drops of the castrated Uranus that fell upon her.
The Furies — Alecto, Tisiphone and Megaera — were born from the drops of blood of the castrated Uranus, keeping to Hesiod's cosmogony.
The three Furies (Alecto, Megaera, Tisiphone) are children of Aether and Terra (Earth), not spirits sprung from Uranus' wound.

quarrels.significance: the avengers of kin-bloodshed have two incompatible origins — born of the primal violence against a father (Hesiod, Apollodorus) versus an ordinary pairing of upper air and earth (Hyginus) — so the very crime they punish either is or is not written into their birth.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Hesiod Theog. 183–187 and Apollodorus Bibliotheca 1.1.4 (Furies from the blood-drops of Uranus) and Hyginus Fabulae preface (Furies as children of Aether and Terra) confirmed against the pinned corpus (Perseus).

quarrels.title: Antaeus' father: Earth or Poseidon?

claims.claim: Antaeus is a son of Terra (Earth) — the Libyan giant Hercules slew, who forced visitors to wrestle and killed them when exhausted.
Antaeus, the giant who ruled Libya and killed strangers by forcing them to wrestle, is a son of Poseidon.

quarrels.significance: the giant's two filiations each anchor a different half of his legend — descent from Earth explains the secret of his strength (he is invincible while he touches his mother), while descent from Poseidon explains the temple of skulls he raises to the sea-god. The sources let the clash stand rather than reconcile it.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Hyginus Fabulae 31 (Antaeus son of Earth) and Apollodorus Bibliotheca 2.5.11 (Antaeus son of Poseidon) confirmed against the pinned corpus (Perseus). Distinct from the Arcadian Argonaut Antaeus, son of Lycurgus (Apollonius, Argonautica 1.161).

quarrels.title: Whose son is the giant Tityos?

claims.claim: Tityos is the son of glorious Gaia (Earth), seen by Odysseus among the punished dead.
Tityos was a son of Zeus and Elare, daughter of Orchomenus; Zeus hid her under the earth for fear of Hera, and there Earth brought the monstrous child to birth.

quarrels.significance: the giant whose crime against Leto defines him is either a pure son of Earth (Homer's stark cosmic monster) or a concealed bastard of Zeus reborn from the ground (Apollodorus' harmonizing version, which still routes the birth through Earth) — so his outrage is either an earth-born sacrilege or, awkwardly, a son's assault on his own father's consort. Apollonius preserves the same compromise: Elare bore him, but Earth nursed him and gave him a second birth (Argonautica 1.761–762).
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Homer Odyssey 11.576 ("Tityos, son of glorious Gaia") and Apollodorus Bibliotheca 1.4.1 (son of Zeus and Elare, brought to birth by Earth) confirmed against the pinned corpus (Perseus); Apollonius Argonautica 1.759–762 corroborates the double-birth harmonization.

quarrels.title: Whose daughters are the Hesperides?

claims.claim: Nyx (Night) bore the Hesperides alone, among her dark brood, to guard the golden apples beyond glorious Ocean — no father named.
The Hesperides are listed among the children of Nox (Night).
The golden apples are kept by the Hesperides, daughters of Atlas, in the garden among the Hyperboreans.

quarrels.significance: the keepers of the golden apples are either fatherless powers of evening sprung from primeval Night (Hesiod, Hyginus) or daughters of the Titan Atlas, anchoring them to the same western edge of the world where he upholds the sky (Apollodorus) — a shift from cosmic abstraction to Titan lineage that mirrors the Moirai's double parentage.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Hesiod Theogony 215–216 (Nyx bears the Hesperides) and Apollodorus Bibliotheca 2.5.11 (daughters of Atlas) confirmed against the pinned corpus (Perseus); Hyginus Fabulae preface lists them under Nox.

quarrels.title: Whose daughter is Styx?

claims.claim: Styx is the eldest and chiefest of the Oceanid daughters of Oceanus and Tethys.
Styx is named among the Oceanids born to Ocean and Tethys.
Styx is listed among the children of Nox (Night) and Erebus.

quarrels.significance: the goddess of the binding oath is either the foremost of the world-encircling river's daughters (Hesiod, Apollodorus), which roots the divine oath in the same Ocean stream a tenth of whose water she is, or a child of primeval Night and Erebus (Hyginus) — recasting the oath-power as a creature of darkness rather than of the cosmic waters, in step with Hyginus' wider habit of routing primordial figures back through Nox.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Hesiod Theogony 361 and 383–385 (eldest Oceanid of Ocean and Tethys) and Apollodorus Bibliotheca 1.2.2 (Oceanid line) confirmed against the pinned corpus (Perseus); Hyginus Fabulae preface lists Styx under Nox and Erebus per the project's pre-verified canonical facts.

quarrels.title: Who was the mother of Rhesus?

claims.claim: Euterpe bore Rhesus, the Thracian king slain by Diomedes at Troy, to the river-god Strymon — "but some say his mother was Calliope."
Knows Rhesus only as the son of Eïoneus, with no Muse as his parent, when Odysseus and Diomedes kill him in his camp by night.

quarrels.significance: the Thracian ally cut down with his white horses on the night raid is, in the mythographic genealogies, the child of a Muse by the river Strymon — and Apollodorus himself cannot settle which Muse, naming Euterpe but admitting the rival claim of her sister Calliope, while Homer's epic gives the king a wholly mortal father in Eïoneus and no divine mother at all.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 1.3.4 carries both the Euterpe parentage and the "some say Calliope" variant in the same sentence; Homer Iliad 10 names Rhesus son of Eïoneus, confirmed against the pinned corpus (Perseus).

quarrels.title: Schedius' father — Iphitus or Perimedes?

claims.claim: In the Catalogue of Ships, Schedius is captain of the Phocians alongside Epistrophus, son of great-souled Iphitus son of Naubolus.
When Hector smites Schedius beneath the collar-bone, he is the son of Iphitus, far the best of the Phocians, king over many men at Panopeus.
In the scattered fight at the ships, Hector slew Schedius son of Perimedes, a leader of the Phocians.

quarrels.significance: Homer names the same Phocian captain twice with different fathers — Iphitus in the muster-roll and Book 17, Perimedes in Book 15 — so the genealogical line behind one Catalog of Ships entry cannot be stated without a dispute badge.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — all three Iliad passages confirmed against the pinned corpus (Perseus); the contradiction is internal to Homer, not an inter-author clash.

quarrels.title: Hippothous' father — Lethus or Pelasgus?

claims.claim: Hippothous and Pylaeus lead the Pelasgi from deep-soiled Larisa as sons twain of Pelasgian Lethus, son of Teutamus.
When Hippothous drags Patroclus by the foot, he is the glorious son of Pelasgian Lethus.
Among the allies who joined the Trojans, Hippothous is son of Pelasgus from Larissa.

quarrels.significance: the Pelasgian captain at Troy has a full three-generation stemma in Homer (Teutamus → Lethus → Hippothous) but a single named father in Apollodorus' ally catalogue — the atlas wires both parent edges under one topic rather than choosing one genealogy.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Iliad 2.820–855, 17.275–315 and Epitome 3.35 confirmed against the pinned corpus (Perseus).

quarrels.title: The death of Thersites

claims.claim: Thersites survives the Iliad — last seen rebuked and beaten at assembly after railing at Agamemnon; the poem ends with Hector's funeral and no further mention of his death.
After Achilles killed Penthesilea, Thersites mocked the hero's grief for the Amazon; Achilles slew him for it.

quarrels.significance: the reviling common soldier whom Homer leaves alive at Troy's end is, in the Epic Cycle aftermath preserved by Apollodorus, killed by Achilles for jeering at his mourning — an Aethiopis episode outside the Iliad itself.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Iliad 2.211–277 (Thersites beaten, no death) against Epitome 5.1 (Achilles slays Thersites after Penthesilea) confirmed against the pinned corpus (Perseus).

quarrels.title: Which Muse mothered the Sirens?

claims.claim: The Sirens are the daughters of the river-god Achelous and the Muse Melpomene.
The Sirens are the daughters of the River Achelous and the Muse Melpomene.
The Sirens are the daughters of Achelous and the Muse Terpsichore, born on the isle Anthemoessa.

quarrels.significance: the parentage of the death-singing Sirens names two different Muses as their mother by the same river-god — Melpomene in the mythographers (Apollodorus, Hyginus) but Terpsichore in Apollonius — so that the choice of Muse, both of them sisters of song, reassigns the Sirens' lethal music to one or the other branch of the Muses' family while leaving Achelous fixed as the father.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Apollodorus Bibliotheca 1.3.4 and Epitome 7.18 (Achelous and Melpomene), Hyginus Fabulae 125 and 141 (Achelous and Melpomene), and Apollonius Argonautica 4.892–896 (Achelous and Terpsichore) confirmed against the pinned corpus (Perseus) and the project's pre-verified canonical facts.

quarrels.title: Was Orpheus the son of the Muse Calliope?

claims.claim: Calliope bore Orpheus (and Linus) to Oeagrus, or nominally to Apollo.
Orpheus, whom Calliope bore wedded to Thracian Oeagrus near the Pimpleian height.
Orpheus is the son of Oeagrus and the Muse Calliope.
It is one of the untruths believed by the Greeks that Orpheus was a son of the Muse Calliope; he was in truth a son of the daughter of Pierus.

quarrels.significance: the mythographic and Argonautic tradition makes the archetypal singer the child of the foremost Muse — a fitting divine pedigree for his irresistible song — but Pausanias singles this very descent out as a popular falsehood, demoting Orpheus' mother from the goddess Calliope to a mortal daughter of Pierus and stripping away the marvels (charmed beasts, the descent to Hades) that the Muse-parentage was held to explain.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Apollodorus Bibliotheca 1.3.2, Apollonius Argonautica 1.23, and Hyginus Fabulae 14 (Calliope as mother) and Pausanias Description of Greece 9.30.4 (the rejection) confirmed against the pinned corpus (Perseus) and the project's pre-verified canonical facts.

quarrels.title: When may Orpheus look back at Eurydice?

claims.claim: Pluto promised Eurydice would follow if Orpheus did not turn until he reached his own house; he disobeyed, beheld his wife, and she turned back.
Eurydice followed up the steep dark path; fearing to lose her at the threshold of earth, Orpheus looked back — and instantly she slipped away.

quarrels.significance: both sources agree that a single backward glance destroys the bargain — but Apollodorus sets the safe limit at Orpheus' own house, while Ovid places the fatal test at the threshold of the upper world, so the distance Eurydice must travel in silence and the exact moment of failure differ between the mythographer's spare account and Ovid's psychologically charged scene.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Apollodorus Bibliotheca 1.3.2 and Ovid Metamorphoses 10.77–95 confirmed against the pinned corpus (Perseus) and the project's pre-verified canonical facts.

quarrels.title: Whose children are the Muses?

claims.claim: The nine Muses are the daughters of Zeus and Mnemosyne (Memory), begotten in Pieria over nine nights.
By Memory (Mnemosyne) Zeus had the Muses — Calliope, Clio, Melpomene, Euterpe, Erato, Terpsichore, Urania, Thalia, and Polymnia.

A Boeotian tradition holds that Pierus, a Macedonian, came to Thespiae and established nine Muses, changing their names to the present ones; others made the figures called children of the Muses really the sons of the daughters of Pierus.

quarrels.significance: the canonical descent of the Muses from Zeus and Mnemosyne — a single divine sisterhood of memory and song shared by Hesiod and the mythographers — is set against a local Boeotian tradition recorded by Pausanias in which the names, and even the parentage, of the nine are the work of the mortal Pierus, so that genealogies elsewhere traced to "a Muse" (the parentage of Linus, of Orpheus) become disputed and locally varying rather than fixed divine descent.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Hesiod Theogony 53–62, 75–79, 915–917 (Zeus and Mnemosyne), Pseudo-Apollodorus Bibliotheca 1.3.1 (the nine borne by Memory to Zeus), and Pausanias Description of Greece 9.29.3–9.29.4 (the Pierus tradition) confirmed against the pinned corpus (Perseus) and the project's pre-verified canonical facts.

quarrels.title: Whose children are the Charites (Graces)?

claims.claim: Eurynome, the daughter of Ocean, bore Zeus three Charites — Aglaia, Euphrosyne, and lovely Thaleia.
By Eurynome, daughter of Ocean, Zeus had the Graces — Aglaia, Euphrosyne, and Thalia.

Hesiod makes the Graces daughters of Zeus and Eurynome under the names Euphrosyne, Aglaia and Thalia; but Antimachus calls them daughters of Aegle and the Sun, and Homer, who knows the Charites, names only Pasithea and a Grace wedded to Hephaestus.

quarrels.significance: the canonical Hesiodic descent of the three named Graces from Zeus and the Oceanid Eurynome — shared by the mythographer Apollodorus — is set against rival ancient accounts that Pausanias collects, in which the Graces are children of Aegle and the Sun (Antimachus) and in which Homer names a wholly different pair (Pasithea, the bride promised to Sleep, and an unnamed Grace married to Hephaestus), so that even the parentage and the very names of the Charites vary by author.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Hesiod Theogony 907–911 (Zeus and Eurynome; "lovely Thaleia"), Pseudo-Apollodorus Bibliotheca 1.3.1 (the three Graces by Eurynome), and Pausanias Description of Greece 9.35.4–9.35.5 (the Hesiodic line plus the Antimachus and Homeric variants) confirmed against the pinned corpus (Perseus) and the project's pre-verified canonical facts.

quarrels.title: What kind of goddess is Hecate?

claims.claim: Hecate is a benevolent universal honorand: Zeus left her the share of earth, sky and sea she held under the older gods, and she favours kings in judgement, warriors, horsemen, fishermen and herdsmen, and nurtures the young.

Hecate is the dread, night-wandering patron of sorcery whom Medea serves as priestess — queen among the dead, propitiated by night at a pit with torches, honey and a black ewe, coming serpent-crowned from the depths when called as Brimo.
Hecate is the three-faced goddess of enchantment and the powers of Night, whose herbs and altars belong to magic and whom Medea and Circe invoke.

quarrels.significance: the same daughter of Perses and Asteria is presented in radically different keys — Hesiod's hymnic, kindly cosmic power whose privilege predates and survives the Olympian order, against the later poets' chthonic, torch-bearing mistress of witchcraft, the dead and the crossroads. The parentage itself is undisputed (Hesiod and Apollodorus agree on Perses and Asteria); what the authors contest is her very nature and sphere.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Hesiod Theogony 404–452 (parentage and the benevolent triple share), Pseudo-Apollodorus Bibliotheca 1.2.4 (Perses and Asteria), Apollonius Argonautica 3.1025–1041, 3.1211 (the night rite, black ewe and Brimo) and 4.829 (mother of Scylla as Crataeis), and Ovid Metamorphoses 7 (the magic patron) confirmed against the pinned corpus (Perseus) and the project's pre-verified canonical facts.

quarrels.title: How many Horae, and who are they?

claims.claim: Themis bore Zeus three Horae — Eunomia (Order), Dike (Justice) and blooming Eirene (Peace), "who mind the works of mortal men."
The Horae, daughters of Jove and Themis, are an expanded set: Auco, Eunomia (Order), Pherusa, Carpo (Fruit), Dike (Justice), Euporia, Eirene (Peace), Orthosie and Thallo.

quarrels.significance: Hesiod's canonical triad of moral-civic Horae — Order, Justice and Peace — is set against the larger, partly seasonal-agricultural catalogue preserved by Hyginus, so that the number and even the membership of the Seasons varies by author; the three Hesiodic sisters (Eunomia, Dike, Eirene) recur in Hyginus's list but are folded into a wider company of Hours.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Hesiod Theogony 901–906 (the three Horae Eunomia, Dike, Eirene) and Hyginus Fabulae 183 (the nine-name catalogue including the same three) confirmed against the pinned corpus (Perseus) and the project's pre-verified canonical facts.

quarrels.title: How did Palamedes die?

claims.claim: The allies stoned Palamedes in the Greek camp at Troy on a forged charge of treason; Agamemnon was Odysseus' accomplice in the murder.
Odysseus forged a letter and buried gold in Palamedes' tent; the allies stoned him as a traitor.
Palamedes was drowned when he put out to catch fish; Diomedes and Odysseus were his murderers.

quarrels.significance: the Epic Cycle and Returns agree that Odysseus hated the counsellor who exposed his feigned madness, but Apollodorus and Hyginus send him to death by stoning in camp while Pausanias, citing the lost Cypria, knows drowning on a fishing expedition — the injustice Nauplius avenges on the fleet is the same, the manner of death is not.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Apollodorus Epitome 3.8, 6.8; Hyginus Fab. 105; Pausanias 10.31.2 confirmed against the pinned corpus (Perseus).

quarrels.title: Nestor's queen: Eurydice or Anaxibia?

claims.claim: Nestor's revered wife at the Pylians' sacrifice is Eurydice, eldest daughter of Clymenus; in the same passage Polycaste, youngest daughter of Nestor, bathes Telemachus.
Thrasymedes is a son of Nestor by Eurydice in the catalogue of Trojan contingents.
Nestor married Anaxibia, daughter of Cratieus, and begot Pisidice, Polycaste, Perseus, Stratichus, Aretus, Echephron, Pisistratus, Antilochus, and Thrasymedes.

quarrels.significance: the queen of sandy Pylos — mother in Apollodorus' full stemma of the princes Homer shows at the feast — bears one name in epic (Eurydice daughter of Clymenus) and another in the mythographer's genealogy (Anaxibia daughter of Cratieus). The same royal household, the same children in later reckoning, but a classic wife-name clash; not to be confused with the homonymous Anaxibia who married Pelias (Bibliotheca 1.9.10).
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Odyssey 3.450–495 (Eurydice wife of Nestor, daughter of Clymenus), Hyginus Fabulae Trojan catalogue (Thrasymedes by Eurydice), and Pseudo-Apollodorus Bibliotheca 1.9.9 (Anaxibia, daughter of Cratieus) confirmed against the pinned corpus (Perseus).

quarrels.title: Pelias' wife

claims.claim: Pelias dwelt in Thessaly and married Anaxibia, daughter of Bias, and begat Acastus and the daughters Pisidice, Pelopia, Hippothoe, and Alcestis — though according to some his wife was Phylomache, daughter of Amphion.
Acastus is son of Pelias and Anaxibia, daughter of Bias, of Iolchus; Alcestis is daughter of Pelias and Anaxibia, Bias' daughter.

quarrels.significance: Apollodorus' primary stemma names Anaxibia daughter of Bias as queen of Iolcus and mother of the Peliades, but the same passage records the alternate wife-name Phylomache daughter of Amphion — a quiet genealogical fork within one author. Not to be confused with the homonymous Anaxibia who married Nestor (Bibliotheca 1.9.9) or the Danaid Anaxibia (`anaxibia-danaid`).
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 1.9.10 and Hyginus Fabulae 14.4, 51 confirmed against the pinned corpus (Perseus).

quarrels.title: Who begot Nausithous?

claims.claim: Nausithous, founder of the Phaeacians on Scheria, was born from Poseidon and Periboea daughter of Eurymedon; he begat Rhexenor and Alcinous.
Calypso was joined to Odysseus in sweet love and bore him Nausithous and Nausinous.
Calypso lay with Odysseus and bore two sons, Nausithous and Telegonus.

quarrels.significance: Homer's Phaeacian founder is a divine son of Poseidon, while Hesiod and Hyginus attach the name Nausithous to sons of Odysseus by Calypso — either a homonym or a competing genealogy for the same legendary name.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Odyssey 7.40–75 (Poseidon and Periboea), Theogony 995–1015 (Calypso and Odysseus), and Hyginus Fabulae 125 confirmed against the pinned corpus (Perseus).

quarrels.title: The parentage of Theoclymenus

claims.claim: Theoclymenus is the son of Polypheides, himself a Melampodid seer made prophet by Apollo after Amphiaraus' death; father and son dwell at Hyperesia in the Argive tradition embedded in Telemachus' voyage.
In the catalogue of augurs, Theoclymenus is son of Proteus (with a garbled aside naming Thestor and Telemus).

quarrels.significance: Telemachus' companion at Pylos and Ithaca is either a named link in Homer's Melampodid prophecy-chain or a figure Hyginus attaches to the Egyptian sea-god Proteus — the same name, two unrelated parentages.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Odyssey 15.225–260 (Polypheides and Theoclymenus) and Hyginus Fabulae 128 (son of Proteus) confirmed against the pinned corpus (Perseus).

quarrels.title: The death of Apsyrtus

claims.claim: Medea murdered her brother Apsyrtus aboard the fleeing Argo, cut him limb from limb, and threw the pieces into the sea so Aeetes would gather the child's limbs and fall behind in pursuit; Zeus later sent storm and demanded purification for the murder.

Apsyrtus is an adult commander who pursues the Argonauts; Medea promises to beguile him to come alone to hear her, Jason lies in ambush on the sacred island of Artemis, and Apsyrtus is slain there — Zeus is wrathful at the ruthless murder and the Argo must be purified by Circe.

quarrels.significance: the same fratricide that delays Aeetes' pursuit is told in two incompatible keys — Pherecydes' child-dismemberment at sea, preserved by Apollodorus, against Apollonius' Hellenistic softening into an adult's ambush on land with Jason as the slayer and Medea as the lure.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 1.9.23–24 (brother aboard ship, limb from limb, Tomi) and Apollonius Argonautica 4.391–481, 4.557 (pursuit, beguilement, Artemis island, Jason's ambush, Zeus' wrath) confirmed against the pinned corpus (Perseus).

quarrels.title: The death of Medea's children at Corinth

claims.claim: Some say Medea herself killed the children she had borne Jason when she fled Corinth after sending the poisoned robe to Glauce.
Another tradition: she left the children still infants as suppliants on the altar of Hera of the Height, and the Corinthians removed them and wounded them to death.
At Corinth the sons Mermerus and Pheres were stoned to death by the Corinthians because of Medea's gifts to Glauce; their tomb stood above the Well of Glauce and the city long offered them cult.

quarrels.significance: the most famous later version (Euripides' deliberate infanticide) is not in the pinned corpus, but the surviving Greek sources already fork on agency — Medea as killer in one Apollodoran strand, the Corinthians as killers in another, with Pausanias naming the victims and grounding the stoning in local cult.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 1.9.28 (both Apollodoran traditions) and Pausanias Description of Greece 2.3.6–7 (Mermerus, Pheres, stoning, tomb) confirmed against the pinned corpus (Perseus).

quarrels.title: Ixion's cloud-mate and the birth of Centaurus

claims.claim: Zeus fashioned a cloud in Hera's likeness; Ixion lay with it and the cloud bore Centaurus.
Ixion's mate is Nubes (the cloud); centaurs such as Nessus are sons of Ixion and Nubes.

quarrels.significance: the progenitor of the wild centaurs is born from a cloud in both traditions, but Apollodorus makes the cloud Zeus' trap in Hera's shape while Hyginus names a distinct cloud-mate Nubes — do not merge with `nephele` the Athamantid cloud.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Epitome 1.20 and Hyginus Fabulae 34 confirmed against the pinned corpus.

quarrels.title: Parentage of Nessus

claims.claim: Nessus is a centaur, son of Ixion and Nubes.
Nessus is son of Centaurus (progenitor of the centaur stock).

quarrels.significance: Hyginus gives direct parentage to Ixion and the cloud; the Centauros-son genealogy is common in later summaries but is not attested in the seven atlas lenses — model Hyginus in data, narrate the other branch in prose on `centauros`.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Hyginus Fabulae 34 confirmed against the pinned corpus.

quarrels.title: Parentage of Endeïs

claims.claim: Endeis is daughter of Sciron.
Endeis is daughter of Chiron; Peleus and Telamon are sons of Aeacus and Endeis.

quarrels.significance: the Aeacid queen's parentage forks between a Megarian warlord and the just centaur — only the Hyginus edge is wired (`chiron` parent `endeis`); Sciron stays prose until promoted.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 3.12.6 and Fabulae 14.2 confirmed against the pinned corpus.

quarrels.title: Parentage of Peirithous

claims.claim: Pirithous is son of Ixion from Larissa.
Peirithous is son of Ixion, brother of Centaurus.
Zeus loved the wife of Ixion, who bore Peirithous; in the Catalogue Polypoetes is son of Peirithous whom immortal Zeus begat.

quarrels.significance: the Lapith king is Ixionid in the genealogies but divinely begotten in Homer — the same double-paternity pattern as Theseus.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 1.8.2, Fabulae 14.2, Iliad 14.317–328 and 2.740–741 confirmed against the pinned corpus.

quarrels.title: Parentage of Amphitrite

claims.claim: Amphitrite is born to Nereus and Doris among the Nereids.
Amphitrite is among the Nereids born to Nereus and Doris.
Amphitrite is among the Oceanids born to Ocean and Tethys.

quarrels.significance: the sea-queen sits in both genealogies — Nereid daughter of the Old Man of the Sea in Hesiod and the Nereid roll, but an Oceanid in Apollodorus' Titan catalogue. The atlas wires both parent sets under the shared topic rather than flattening her to one line.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Theogony 240–264 and Bibliotheca 1.2.2, 1.2.7 confirmed against the pinned corpus.

quarrels.title: Mother of Tyndareus, Hippocoon, and Icarius

claims.claim: Gorgophone, daughter of Perseus, bore Tyndareus, Icarius, Aphareus, and Leucippus to Perieres (or, in Pausanias, to Oebalus).
Oebalus begat Tyndareus, Hippocoon, and Icarius by the Naiad nymph Batia.

quarrels.significance: the Spartan royal house forks not only on whether Tyndareus is son of Perieres or of Oebalus (`tyndareus-parentage`), but on whether his mother is a Perseid princess or a Laconian Naiad — the same fork that decides Hippocoon and Icarius' maternity.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 3.10.3–3.10.4 confirmed against the pinned corpus.

quarrels.title: Mother of Lycaon

claims.claim: Pelasgus begat Lycaon by Meliboea, daughter of Ocean.
Pelasgus begat Lycaon by a nymph named Cyllene.

quarrels.significance: at the very root of the Arcadian royal house, Lycaon's maternity forks between an Oceanid princess and a mountain nymph of Cyllene — the same peak later famed as Hermes' birthplace and as the Pleiads' birth-mountain.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 3.8.1 confirmed against the pinned corpus.

quarrels.title: Actaeon's offense

claims.claim: Zeus was angry at Actaeon because he wooed Semele.
Actaeon saw Artemis bathing and was punished for it.
Actaeon boasted himself the better hunter.
Actaeon saw Diana bathing, desired her, and Diana set horns on his head so his own dogs tore him apart.
Actaeon wandered into Gargaphie, saw Diana bathing, and was transformed into a stag until his hounds ran him down.

quarrels.significance: Apollodorus preserves three incompatible charges against the hunter grandson of Cadmus without choosing among them — the Semele-wooing strand ties Actaeon's ruin to the Theban house's divine affairs, while Hyginus and Ovid fix the offense on the sacred bath of Artemis alone.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 3.4.4 confirmed against the pinned corpus; Hyginus and Ovid bath-narratives align with `actaeon-artemis`.

quarrels.title: Regional affiliation of Smyrna

claims.claim: Smyrna was one of the twelve Aeolian cities on the coast, on the site later called the old town.
Ionians from Colophon displaced the Aeolians and later admitted Smyrna to the Ionian assembly at Panionium; elsewhere Pausanias calls the Smyrnaeans an Ionian people.

quarrels.significance: the city's ethnic label forks within the atlas lenses — geographic metadata prefers the Aeolian sub-region (`aeolis`), while Pausanias also records its Ionian membership and Ionian resettlement.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Description of Greece 7.5.1 and 4.21.5 confirmed against the pinned corpus.

quarrels.title: Parentage of Peirene

claims.claim: Peirene is daughter of Achelous; by Poseidon she bore Leches and Cenchrias, eponyms of Corinth's harbours.
In the poem called the Great Eoeae, Peirene is said to be a daughter of Oebalus.

quarrels.significance: the Corinthian spring nymph's genealogy forks within a single Pausanias passage — Achelous' river-house versus the Spartan/Laconian stem of Oebalus — without either line being dismissed.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Description of Greece 2.2.3 confirmed against the pinned corpus.

quarrels.title: Children of Endymion

claims.claim: Endymion had by a Naiad nymph — or, as some say, by Iphianassa — a son Aetolus.
Endymion begat Paeon, Epeius, Aetolus, and Eurycyda by a mortal wife — Asterodia, or Cromia daughter of Itonus, or Hyperippe daughter of Arcas.

quarrels.significance: Aetolus' maternity forks three ways — unnamed Naiad, named princess Iphianassa, or one of Pausanias' mortal queens — while all strands agree Endymion fathered the eponym of Aetolia.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 1.7.6 and Description of Greece 5.1.4 confirmed against the pinned corpus.

quarrels.title: Mother of Bucolion

claims.claim: Laomedon begat a son Bucolion by a nymph Calybe.

Bucolion was son of lordly Laomedon, his eldest born, though the mother that bare him was unwed; while shepherding his flocks he lay with the fountain-nymph Abarbarea, who bare twin sons Aesepus and Pedasus.

quarrels.significance: Apollodorus names Calybe as Bucolion's mother in the king's prose genealogy, while Homer's battle narrative leaves Bucolion's birth-mother unnamed and introduces Abarbarea only as his lover and mother of the twins — two fountain-nymph strands in the Laomedon stemma that the atlas keeps as rival lines rather than merged identities.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 3.12.3 and Iliad 6.1–35 confirmed against the pinned corpus.

quarrels.title: Parentage of Callisto

claims.claim: Callisto is the daughter of Lycaon, who ruled in Arcadia.
Callisto is one of the nymphs.
Callisto is a daughter of Nycteus.
Callisto is a daughter of Ceteus.
The maiden of the Great Bear is Callisto, daughter of Lycaon who ruled in Arcadia, citing Hesiod as authority.
Lycaon had a daughter Callisto, loved by Zeus and turned into a bear by Hera.

quarrels.significance: at the root of the Arcadian bear-myth, Callisto's maternity forks between a Lycaonid princess and several nymph or collateral-royal lines that Apollodorus records without choosing among them — the Hesiodic nymph strand underpins her `oread` kind, while Pausanias and Hyginus keep the Lycaonid default.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 3.8.2, Astronomica 2.1.1, and Description of Greece 8.3.6 confirmed against the pinned corpus.

quarrels.title: Consort and maternity of Arcas' sons

claims.claim: Arcas' wife was no mortal woman but a Dryad nymph named Erato, by whom he had Azan, Apheidas, and Elatus.
Arcas had two sons, Elatus and Aphidas, by Leanira daughter of Amyclas.
The same sons were born of Meganira daughter of Croco.
The same sons were born of a nymph Chrysopelia.

quarrels.significance: Pausanias' Dryad marriage gives Arcas three eponymous sons including Azan, while Apollodorus' roll names only Elatus and Aphidas and forks their mother three ways — mortal Leanira, mortal Meganira, or the nymph Chrysopelia — without harmonizing the son-lists.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Description of Greece 8.4.2 and Bibliotheca 3.9.1 confirmed against the pinned corpus.

quarrels.title: Mother of Sarpedon

claims.claim: Sarpedon, captain of the Lycians at Troy, is the son of Zeus and Laodameia, daughter of Bellerophon.

Europa bore Zeus three sons in Crete — Minos, Sarpedon, and Rhadamanthys — "but according to Homer, Sarpedon was a son of Zeus by Laodamia, daughter of Bellerophon"; driven out by Minos, this Sarpedon became king of Lycia, and Zeus granted him to live for three generations.
Sarpedon, whom Patroclus slew, is the son of Jove and Europa, brother of Minos and Rhadamanthus.

quarrels.significance: Zeus is the father everywhere, but the mother moves Sarpedon across two generations and two houses — a grandson of Bellerophon in Homer, a brother of Minos in the mythographers. Apollodorus records Homer's version himself and bridges the gap with a life three generations long, so the atlas keeps one `sarpedon` star and tags the two mothers instead of splitting the figure.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Iliad 6.198–199 (English and Greek), Bibliotheca 3.1.1–3.1.2, and Fabulae 106, 155, 178 confirmed against the pinned corpus. The `sarpedon-parent-europa` edge previously listed `homer` among its sources; Homer never names Europa as Sarpedon's mother, so that attribution was removed.

quarrels.title: Heracles on the Argo

claims.claim: Heracles joins the Argo of his own will, straight from carrying the Erymanthian boar alive to Mycenae; he is left behind in Mysia searching for Hylas, destined to go back to the labours of Eurystheus.
The Argonauts left Heracles and Polyphemus in Mysia when Hylas was carried off by the nymphs.
Heracles did not sail at all at that time; he was serving as a slave at the court of Omphale.
He was left behind at Aphetae in Thessaly, the Argo having declared with a human voice that she could not bear his weight.
Heracles sailed all the way to Colchis — Dionysius even makes him the leader of the Argonauts.
Hercules is counted among the Argonauts, with Hylas as his companion.

quarrels.significance: where the voyage falls in Heracles' life orders the heroic age. If he sails in the midst of his labours (Apollonius, the main line of Apollodorus), the Argo comes before his servitude to Omphale, his wrestling for Deianira and his death; on Herodorus' reckoning the voyage and the Lydian servitude run together. The atlas's time axis follows the voyage-within-the-labours line — the death of Heracles is dated after the Argo in `data/chronology.json` — while `omphale-and-troy` keeps the Herodorus strand in view.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Argonautica 1.122, 1.1273, 1.1296 and 1.1344, Bibliotheca 1.9.19 and Fabulae 14 confirmed against the pinned corpus.

quarrels.title: Who killed Coronis?

claims.claim: Apollo himself shoots Coronis through the breast; repenting too late, he tears his unborn son from her womb on the pyre and carries him to Chiron's cave.
Apollo kills Coronis and, while she burns, snatches the babe from the pyre and brings him to Chiron.
Apollo strikes Coronis and takes Asclepius from her womb; her lover Ischys dies by Jove's thunderbolt — or, in the star-myths, by Apollo's arrows.
Artemis kills Coronis to avenge the insult to her brother, and Hermes snatches the infant from the pyre already alight.

quarrels.significance: the god who loved her is her killer in the poet and the mythographers, while the tradition Pausanias heard gives the killing to Artemis and the rescue to Hermes — and within Hyginus even Ischys dies two different deaths.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Metamorphoses 2.600–632 line-checked in the Latin; Bibliotheca 3.10.3 and Description of Greece 2.26.6 in the Greek; Fabulae 202 and Astronomica 2.40.2 in the corpus English.

quarrels.title: Who was the mother of Asclepius?

claims.claim: Arsinoe, daughter of Leucippus, bore Asclepius to Apollo; "some say" his mother was Coronis, daughter of Phlegyas, in Thessaly.

The Epidaurians say Phlegyas' daughter bore him in secret in their land and exposed him on Mount Titthion; the Messenians claim him as Arsinoe's son, which Pausanias judges the least true, citing the Pythia's verse that Coronis bore him in rocky Epidaurus.
Divine Coronis bore him in bright Lacereia, at the outflow of the Thessalian Amyrus.
His mother is Coronis of Larisa in Haemonia.

quarrels.significance: Thessaly, Epidaurus and Messenia each claimed the healer's birth. The Messenian version makes him a Leucippid and gives Messenia his sons; the Delphic verse Pausanias quotes settles it for Epidaurus, the seat of his greatest sanctuary.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 3.10.3 and Description of Greece 2.26.3–7 in the Greek, 4.3.2 in the corpus English; Argonautica 4.616–617 and 1.596 line-checked in the Greek; Metamorphoses 2.542 in the Latin.

quarrels.title: Whom did Asclepius raise, and who revived Glaucus?

claims.claim: With the Gorgon's blood Asclepius raised Capaneus, Lycurgus, Hippolytus, Tyndareus, Hymenaeus and Glaucus son of Minos; yet in the Cretan saga it is the seer Polyidus who revives the drowned Glaucus with a herb a serpent showed him.
Asclepius is said to have restored Glaucus or Hippolytus and was struck by the thunderbolt for it; the fable of Glaucus gives the revival to Polyidus and the serpent's herb.
Hippolytus, reborn as Virbius, owes his second life to the strong medicine of Apollo's son.
An old slab at Epidaurus records twenty horses Hippolytus dedicated to the god, and the Aricians say Asclepius raised him.

quarrels.significance: the same resurrection of a Cretan prince is credited both to the healer-god's son and to a mortal seer, and the mythographers cannot agree which raising — Glaucus' or Hippolytus' — brought down the thunderbolt that killed Asclepius.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 3.10.3 in the Greek and 3.3.1 in the corpus English; Fabulae 49 and 136 and Astronomica 2.14.6 in the corpus English; Metamorphoses 15.531–535 in the Latin; Description of Greece 2.27.4 in the Greek.

quarrels.title: Did Heracles kill Augeas?

claims.claim: Heracles took Elis, killed Augeas and his sons, and brought Phyleus back from exile to give him the kingdom.

Heracles gave Elis to Phyleus out of respect for him but left Augeas unpunished; Phyleus set the realm in order and went back to Dulichium, and Augeas died in old age — the Eleans still sacrifice to him as a hero.

quarrels.significance: the king whose broken bargain started the war either dies with his sons or lives on to be honoured as a hero of Elis, and Phyleus either rules a conquered kingdom or restores his father's house and leaves. The Phyleus reign in `data/lineages/pisa-elis.json` carries the same topic.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 2.7.2 and Description of Greece 5.3.1–3 and 5.4.2 in the Greek.

quarrels.title: Why and where did Heracles sack Pylos — and did Neleus survive?

claims.claim: Neleus had refused to purify Heracles after the murder of Iphitus; Heracles took Pylos, killed Neleus and all his sons but Nestor, then being reared among the Gerenians, and wounded Hades, who fought for the Pylians.
Heracles killed Neleus and ten of his sons because Neleus would not purify him after he had killed Megara and her children.
Heracles crushed Pylos and of Neleus' twelve sons only Nestor was left — yet in Nestor's tale Neleus still reigns; Hades took Heracles' arrow "at Pylos among the dead".
The Eleans say it was at their own Pylos, in Elis, that Hades fought against Heracles, with Athena on Heracles' side — and that is why they alone honour Hades.

quarrels.significance: the sack of Nestor's home either wipes out the Neleid house but for its youngest son or leaves the old king on his throne; the purification Neleus refused has two different victims behind it; and the Eleans moved the battle, wounded god and all, to their own Pylos.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 2.6.2 and 2.7.3 in the Greek; Iliad 11.682–693, 11.717 and 5.395–402 line-checked in the Greek; Description of Greece 6.25.2–3 in the Greek; Fabulae 10 and 31 in the corpus English.

quarrels.title: Did Periclymenus escape Heracles?

claims.claim: Poseidon's gift let Periclymenus turn into a lion, a snake or a bee, but Heracles killed him with the rest of Neleus' sons.
Having tried every shape in vain, Periclymenus became an eagle; Hercules' arrow caught him where wing meets side, and he fell to his death.
His grandfather Neptune turned Periclymenus into an eagle, and he escaped the siege alive.

quarrels.significance: the shape-shifter is either the last and hardest kill of the sack of Pylos or, with Nestor, the only son of Neleus to survive it.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 1.9.9 and 2.7.3 in the Greek; Metamorphoses 12.556–572 line-checked in the Latin; Fabulae 10 in the corpus English.

quarrels.title: Where did Iphicles die?

claims.claim: Iphicles fell in Heracles' war on Hippocoon and his sons at Sparta, together with Cepheus of Tegea and his sons.
Iphicles was wounded by the sons of Actor in Heracles' first battle against Augeas, was carried to Pheneus, and died and was buried there.

quarrels.significance: Heracles' mortal twin falls either in the Spartan campaign that restored Tyndareus or, earlier, of a wound from the Elean war — two different wars for the same death.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 2.7.3 and Description of Greece 8.14.9 in the Greek.

quarrels.title: Were the daughters of Leucippus stolen brides?

claims.claim: The Dioscuri carried off Hilaira and Phoebe, daughters of Leucippus, from Messene and married them; Phoebe bore Mnesileus to Polydeuces and Hilaira bore Anogon to Castor. No betrothal to the sons of Aphareus is mentioned.
Phoebe and Hilaira, priestesses of Minerva and Diana, were already betrothed to Idas and Lynceus when Castor and Pollux, burning with love, carried them off.
The Tyndarid brothers carried off Phoebe and her sister, and both sons of Aphareus, each pledged to Leucippus as a son-in-law, armed to win them back.
The poet of the Cypria called Hilaira and Phoebe daughters of Apollo; at Argos their images stood beside the twins and two sons named Anaxis and Mnasinous.

quarrels.significance: the Dioscuri either take unattached brides or steal their cousins' promised wives, which makes the feud a war over women; and the sisters' father and the names of their sons change with the teller.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 3.10.3 and 3.11.2 and Description of Greece 3.16.1 and 2.22.5 in the Greek; Fabulae 80 in the Latin (The Latin Library); Fasti 5.699–702 in the Latin (The Latin Library) — the Fasti is outside the pinned corpus.

quarrels.title: What set the Dioscuri against the sons of Aphareus?

claims.claim: The four cousins raided cattle in Arcadia; Idas, left to divide the herd, won it all by a trick with a quartered cow and drove it to Messene, and the Dioscuri marched on Messene, drove off the herd and much besides, and lay in wait.
The cousins fought over cattle.
Idas and Lynceus fought to recover the brides Castor and Pollux had carried off.
The brothers armed to reclaim the promised brides; love drove one pair to demand and the other to refuse, so each fought with equal right.

quarrels.significance: the fatal fight is either a quarrel among cattle-raiders over a cheated share or a war of rival bridegrooms — plunder or love as the cause of the Dioscuri's mortal end.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 3.11.2 and Description of Greece 4.3.1 in the Greek; Fabulae 80 and Fasti 5.699–706 in the Latin (The Latin Library; the Fasti is outside the pinned corpus).

quarrels.title: Who killed whom when the Dioscuri fought the sons of Aphareus?

claims.claim: Lynceus spied Castor in ambush and Idas killed him; Polydeuces speared Lynceus and, chasing Idas, was stunned by a stone before Zeus struck Idas with a thunderbolt.
Polydeuces killed Lynceus, and Idas was struck by lightning.
Lynceus' sword pierced Castor's chest; Pollux speared Lynceus, and Idas was barely driven back by Jupiter's fire.

Castor killed Lynceus; when Castor tried to stop Idas raising a tomb for his brother, Idas drove his sword into Castor's groin, and Pollux killed Idas in single combat. Castor is also said to have died at Aphidnae, in a war of the Lacedaemonians against the Athenians, or when Idas and Lynceus attacked Sparta.

quarrels.significance: every pairing of killer and victim shifts — Castor falls to Idas or to Lynceus, Lynceus to Polydeuces or to Castor, Idas to Zeus' bolt or to Pollux' hand. Every slayer edge of the fight carries this topic, each tagged with the tellers who make it.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 3.11.2 and Description of Greece 4.3.1 in the Greek (the corpus English of Bibliotheca 3.11.2 says "pursuing Lynceus", but the Greek has Polydeuces pursuing Idas); Fabulae 80 and Astronomica 2.22 in the Latin (The Latin Library); Fasti 5.707–714 in the Latin (The Latin Library; outside the pinned corpus).

quarrels.title: How do the Dioscuri share immortality?

claims.claim: The life-giving earth holds both alive; beneath the earth, honoured by Zeus, they live on alternate days and are dead on the others, with honour equal to the gods'.
Taken up to heaven, Polydeuces refused immortality while Castor was dead, so Zeus let both be every other day among the gods and among mortals.
Jupiter gave a star to Pollux alone, as Castor was Tyndareus' son, until Pollux asked to share it with his brother; the Twins are set in the sky for their devotion.
Pollux pleads that half the gift is worth more than the whole, and the brothers keep their stations by turns as stars that help ships in distress.

quarrels.significance: the alternation is constant, but where the twins spend their days is not — under the earth in Homer, between Olympus and the mortal world in Apollodorus, among the stars in Hyginus and Ovid.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Odyssey 11.301–304 line-checked in the Greek; Bibliotheca 3.11.2 in the Greek; Fabulae 80 and Astronomica 2.22 in the Latin (The Latin Library); Fasti 5.715–720 in the Latin (The Latin Library; outside the pinned corpus).

quarrels.title: How did Antiope come back from Sicyon?

claims.claim: Pregnant by Zeus and threatened by her father, Antiope fled to Epopeus at Sicyon and married him; Nycteus killed himself in despair, charging his brother Lycus to punish them, and Lycus took Sicyon, killed Epopeus and led Antiope away captive.
Nycteus, dying, bound his brother Lycus by oath to punish her and left him the kingdom; the Sicyonian who took her in is called Epaphus, and Antiope is brought back in bonds.

Epopeus carried Antiope off, whether after courting her or by force; Nycteus, wounded in the war that followed, made Lycus regent for the boy Labdacus before he died; Epopeus died of a neglected wound, and his successor Lamedon gave Antiope up without a fight.

quarrels.significance: Antiope either runs to Sicyon or is carried there, her father dies by his own hand or of a battle wound, and Epopeus is killed by Lycus or dies of a neglected wound — three routes to the same captivity.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 3.5.5 and Description of Greece 2.6.1–3 in the Greek; Fabulae 8 in the corpus English and the Latin (Lingua Latina Legenda), which reads Epaphus for the Sicyonian.

quarrels.title: What became of Lycus?

claims.claim: Amphion and Zethus killed Lycus and tied Dirce to a bull.
The twins overcame Lycus in battle and took the kingdom; his death is not told.
As the brothers were about to kill Lycus, Mercury stopped them and ordered Lycus to yield the kingdom to Amphion.

quarrels.significance: the usurper of Thebes is executed, merely overthrown, or spared by a god's command — Hyginus' telling, after Euripides' Antiope, ends in divine intervention rather than vengeance.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 3.5.5 and Description of Greece 9.5.6 in the Greek; Fabulae 8 in the corpus English and the Latin (Lingua Latina Legenda).

quarrels.title: How did the house of Amphion end?

claims.claim: Artemis and Apollo shot down Amphion's children after Niobe's boast; after Amphion's death Laius took the kingdom.
In his list of Theban kings, plague emptied Amphion's house; Zethus' son died through some error of his mother, Zethus died of grief, and the Thebans brought Laius back.
Pandareus' daughter, the nightingale, mourns Itylus, son of lord Zethus, whom she killed unwitting.

quarrels.significance: the end of the twin kings' line is either the gods' punishment of Niobe's pride or a plague and a household accident — and Pausanias, who records the Niobids' arrows and tombs elsewhere, follows the plague in his king-list.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 3.5.6–7 and Description of Greece 9.5.9 in the Greek; Odyssey 19.518–523 line-checked in the Greek.

quarrels.title: Who took Chrysippus, and how did Hippodamia end?

claims.claim: Laius, Pelops' guest in his exile, fell in love with Chrysippus while teaching him to drive a chariot and carried him off.

Laius seized Chrysippus, Pelops' bastard son, at the Nemean games, and Pelops recovered him by war; Atreus and Thyestes, urged on by Hippodamia, killed him, and when Pelops blamed her she killed herself. Another list names Theseus as the one who carried Chrysippus off from the games.
Hippodamia withdrew to Midea in the Argolid because of Pelops' anger over Chrysippus' death; the Eleans later brought her bones to Olympia at an oracle's bidding.

quarrels.significance: the first crime of the Pelopid house has two abductors and two ends for the queen — suicide under her husband's accusation, or exile at Midea and a precinct at Olympia.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Bibliotheca 3.5.5 and Description of Greece 6.20.7 in the Greek; Fabulae 85, 243 and 271 in the corpus English.

quarrels.title: How was Aegisthus conceived?

claims.claim: An oracle told Thyestes that a son begotten on his own daughter would avenge him, and he obeyed and begot Aegisthus by her; the daughter is not named.

Thyestes, a fugitive at King Thesprotus' court, came by night to Sicyon and, his head veiled, forced his daughter Pelopia as she washed her robe after a sacrifice to Minerva; Atreus, taking her for Thesprotus' daughter, married her while she carried the child, and reared the exposed Aegisthus, suckled by a goat, as his own.

quarrels.significance: the avenger of the feast is begotten either by deliberate incest at an oracle's command or by a rape in the dark at Sicyon — and in Hyginus the son grows up in his victim's house as Atreus' own.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Epitome 2.14 in the Greek; Fabulae 87–88 and 252 in the corpus English, with Fabula 88 also checked in the Latin (The Latin Library).

quarrels.title: How did Atreus die, and what became of Thyestes?

claims.claim: Agamemnon and Menelaus seized Thyestes at Delphi; Atreus sent Aegisthus to kill him in prison, but Thyestes knew the sword, Pelopia killed herself with it, and Aegisthus killed Atreus as he sacrificed on the shore and returned with his father to the ancestral kingdom.

The grown Aegisthus learned who his father was, killed Atreus and restored Thyestes; a nurse carried Atreus' sons to Polyphides of Sicyon and on to Oeneus in Aetolia, until Tyndareus brought them back, Thyestes was sent under oath to Cythera, and Agamemnon ruled Mycenae.
At his death Atreus left the sceptre to Thyestes, and Thyestes in turn left it to Agamemnon to bear as lord of many islands and all Argos.

quarrels.significance: Atreus falls to the son he reared in every version that tells his death, but the Atreids' road back runs through exile and Tyndareus' help in Apollodorus, while in Hyginus they are grown men who hunt Thyestes down themselves — and Homer's sceptre simply passes from brother to brother to son.
quarrels.verification: ✓ verified — Epitome 2.14 and 2.16 in the Greek, with Epitome 2.15 read as Frazer's supplement from Tzetzes (Chiliades 1.456–465); Fabulae 88 in the Latin (The Latin Library) and 243 in the corpus English; Iliad 2.105–108 line-checked in the Greek.
